items.body: “There are black silences, like thunderclouds, that burst into flashes of music,” H. G. Wells writes in Select Conversations with an Uncle. The phrase finds an almost literal visual counterpart in Jordan Reyes’s cover for Songs for Sad Poets Vol. III: a dense black expanse pressing against a bleached, nearly featureless sky, its uneven boundary resembling storm clouds seen in negative. It also anticipates a pivotal moment in “Sigils of Decay”, when the music comes to such an abrupt halt that, on first hearing, I had to check whether it was still playing. Out of that prolonged absence a low rumble eventually emerges, giving voice to the disquiet that runs through the latest collaboration between Siavash Amini & Eugene Thacker. The three pieces included are dedicated respectively to Vietnamese poet Hàn Mặc Tử, Brazilian Symbolist João da Cruz e Sousa and Austrian poet Nikolaus Lenau, figures connected by the tradition of the poète maudit. “Leprous Doubt”, for Hàn Mặc Tử, opens with dissonant textures, degraded sounds and sudden changes of register. It is unsettling and unsettled, meandering in unforeseen directions and making its discomfort palpable. The music pauses and resumes, pitching antagonistic forces against one another; moments of sweeping grandeur coexist with passages of intimate travail. It repeatedly attempts to steady itself before faltering again. Circular tones eventually lift to reveal the “glowing abyss” of Thacker’s poem, while intensifying drones recede until a solitary, quivering tone remains. “Sigils of Decay”, for Cruz e Sousa, pushes this instability into silence itself. The long interruption at its centre makes the eventual return of sound unusually physical. As the low frequencies slowly reassert themselves, muted fragments accumulate into a dark, suspended mass. Thacker writes of “muted music / woven by / night spiders”, an image that seems uncannily close to what Amini constructs: strands of sound gradually spun into a crepuscular firmament of drones and disarticulated fragments, only to loosen again. The connection with Cruz e Sousa is equally suggestive. His poetry transforms an inexplicable melancholy into a confrontation with the Infinite; Thacker condenses that metaphysical sadness into the colder “Dread of / Infinite space. / Dread of / Distant skies.” At nineteen minutes, “Dead Eyes, Dark Stars” is the album’s most expansive piece. Its opening is nocturnal, with celestial voices suspended above slumbering coils of sound. These gradually precipitate into increasingly abrasive textures, yet the music pulls itself back towards a softer harmonic balance. Timbral shifts become more pronounced as the underlying material turns metallic and resonant. Lenau’s recurring world of night, forests, barren landscapes, grief and death finds an oblique counterpart here: the landscape seems to have been emptied of narrative and retained as atmosphere, shadow and distant light. Voice assumes a much greater presence than on the first Songs for Sad Poets, although words never present themselves as intelligible text. Synthetic voices gather into spectral choirs and dissolve into the surrounding music, allowing Thacker’s poems to remain embedded within the pieces without requiring the listener to follow them line by line. The relationship between poetry and sound consequently operates through images, structures and emotional pressure: Hàn Mặc Tử’s diseased bodies and impossible skies, Cruz e Sousa’s metaphysical melancholy, Lenau’s nocturnal desolation. Each piece finally leaves a coda of silence. By then, Reyes’s cover feels increasingly inseparable from the music: darkness occupies most of the field, while its opposite persists beyond its ragged edge. H.G. Wells’s “black silences” provide an apt description of an album where silence continually threatens to swallow the music, yet also provides the space from which it can begin again. To lift the veil on the production process we have spoken directly to Saivash Amini. On the first Songs for Sad Poets, Eugene Thacker’s poems were never actually spoken; the words were translated into sound without becoming voice. On Vol. III, you take almost the opposite route, programming voice-synthesis software to perform the poems and then processing as many as forty voices until language becomes unintelligible. What interested you in bringing the human voice into the project only to erase its legibility again? Do you still think of these pieces as songs, or has the distinction between voice, text and sound become irrelevant? The idea of voice synthesis came out of a conversation with Eugene about his dislike of the human voice and the vocal music he actually liked like Ligeti’s requiem, where micropolyphony, among other techniques, were used to mask the intelligibility of the text and transform the human choir into something entirely different. I have much of the liberty of a large choir in my DAW with voice synthesis software. It’s not actually a human voice, so I can make a sound very modulated and affected when singing. And I can have as many as I want to have, as long as my CPU can handle it, so micropolyphony can be much more extreme and differently intricate. And yes, I do think of these as songs, they are structured around the poem. Just not conventional songs with known musical structures. But that’s when I’m making them. There’s no point trying to find the points of reference to poems if you’re just listening, they are trying to convey the same thing. Listening closely to the three pieces, decay seems to function as a compositional process rather than simply as an atmosphere. “Leprous Doubt” repeatedly loses substance and regains it; “Sigils of Decay” moves through accumulation and withdrawal; and the nineteen-minute “Dead Eyes, Dark Stars” forms large masses of sound that gradually weather away, return and finally disappear. This concern with appearance, erosion and reconstitution also seems connected to Eidolon, Caligo and Severed Like the Red Moon, where sounds are made to float, bleed, collapse, be mutilated and reassembled. Has this become a central way for you to think about musical form? Yes and no, I have been more and more putting focus in making structures and out evolving and directional textures made out of different approaches to generating harmony. It’s not all I think about when making pieces but more likely the result of intentional putting together of smaller directional elements of different duration. So the micro is what determines the macro, and a lot of the times I’m thinking of micro. The poets invoked on Vol. III come from very different linguistic and cultural histories: Hàn Mặc Tử and Vietnam’s “Chaos” school, João da Cruz e Sousa and Brazilian Symbolism, and Nikolaus Lenau and the tradition of Weltschmerz. How did you and Eugene Thacker arrive at these particular figures, and what drew you to bringing such different poetic traditions together within the same musical cycle? That’s all Eugene’s side of the project but the thread that links them all is in the Poet Maudit term which the title comes from. They all fit that category. Much of your recent work has begun from literary or historical material: Ibn Sina on eremos, Xavier Villaurrutia on The Sweat of Earth, early Iranian piano recordings and Malakoot on Caligo, as well as Houshang Golshiri on Severed Like the Red Moon. In each case, the source seems to act less as something to illustrate than as a force that changes the way you treat sound. What does literature give you that a purely musical starting point does not, and has worked so closely with Eugene Thacker altered the way you now read a text as a composer? Using literature for my work goes to my first album. Then I have three collaborations with Matt Finney which were based on his reading his poems and sending them to me. Serus had a strong relationship with the writings of Blanchot I can go on… I find using literature gives me a structure and image which I can turn into sound worlds. I can imagine something to convey that image. I find that very exciting but a lot of background work before the project starts is done on purely musical material. Working with Eugene changed my workflow in general and made my relationship with literature deeper than it was before, and it gave me a lot to think about when it comes to making sound that conveys what one word is telling me. (Gianmarco Del Re)
items._genre: dark ambient / drone / experimental / contemporary classical
items._cn_summary: 这是Siavash Amini与Eugene Thacker合作的《Songs for Sad Poets》第三卷，三首作品分别献给三位poète maudit诗人：越南的Hàn Mặc Tử、巴西象征主义者Cruz e Sousa、奥地利诗人Lenau。专辑以不和谐织体、降质音色与突然的力度变化开篇，融合Thacker的诗歌朗诵与Amini的电子声景设计。音乐频繁在沉默与爆发之间切换，长时段的留白使声音的回归具有强烈的物理感。低频嗡鸣与碎片化声响逐渐编织成暮色般的音场，呼应Thacker诗中对无限空间的恐惧。末曲以夜空的声学意象展开，尖锐的金属质感与柔和的泛音层交替涌现，将叙事剥离为纯粹氛围。整张专辑在暗黑氛围、无人机音乐与实验电子之间构建了独特的诗学对话。

items.album: Anushka Chkheidze + Robert Lippok :: The Sky Was Out of Tune (Morr Music)
items.excerpt: Natural recordings, soft rhythms, distortion, metallic noises, melody, and digital artifacts continually lean against one another without settling. By the end it feels less like eight compositions and more like half an hour spent inside a system that was continuously adjusting itself while you were listening, and never quite finished. Everything feels connected by residue The Sky Was Out of Tune by Anushka Chkheidze + Robert Lippok   Anushka Chkheidze and Robert Lippok make sense together.
items.body: Natural recordings, soft rhythms, distortion, metallic noises, melody, and digital artifacts continually lean against one another without settling. By the end it feels less like eight compositions and more like half an hour spent inside a system that was continuously adjusting itself while you were listening, and never quite finished. Everything feels connected by residue The Sky Was Out of Tune by Anushka Chkheidze + Robert Lippok   Anushka Chkheidze and Robert Lippok make sense together. Chkheidze is a Georgian composer and producer based in the Netherlands. Lippok is Berlin, To Rococo Rot, Raster Noton, installation work, decades of treating electronic sound as material that gets layered, cut, reshaped, and left partially unresolved. They met in Tbilisi in 2019 through a workshop program, worked together on Glacier Music II, then built that into Uncontrollable Thoughts, their first joint album for Morr Music in 2025. Morr Music has spent decades in that specific space between electronica, ambient, post-rock, and minimal composition—múm, The Notwist, B. Fleischmann, music where texture and atmosphere carry as much weight as conventional structure. A natural home for this collaboration. The Sky Was Out of Tune pushes further. Eight pieces, titled only with Roman numerals, and they really don’t function as separate tracks so much as sections of one continuous object. That makes sense, the music grew out of a live performance at Berlin’s Neue Nationalgalerie. Everything feels connected by residue. A texture disappears and something remains behind it. A rhythmic idea dissolves into ambience. A metallic sound becomes the thing guiding the next section without announcing itself as such. “I” opens with what sounds like field recording, natural ambience, small bell-like tones, rattling, paper movement, objects handled close to a microphone. Hard to identify exactly what some of those sounds are. Records that begin this way can immediately position themselves as documentary field recording works where the environment becomes the subject. Here the material behaves differently. It’s preparation. Those sounds establish a physical space before synthetic material gets pushed into it. Tiny rhythmic impulses sit beneath the surface :: That becomes one of the strongest ideas running through the record. Chkheidze and Lippok are extremely good at preparing the listener for something before revealing what it is. Ambience gathers density. Distortion arrives gradually. Tiny rhythmic impulses sit beneath the surface before becoming clearer. Metallic sounds enter and disappear like objects moving through the stereo field. No obvious drops. No resolutions. They build toward changes in texture instead, which is a harder thing to make feel earned. Their process on Uncontrollable Thoughts involved long improvisations, selecting ideas afterward, sending projects between one another. Chkheidze contributing drums, piano, vocals. Lippok adding noise, harmony, sometimes reshaping the entire piece. He’s described his production as primarily layering, constructing, collaging, not sitting at a keyboard writing chord progressions. You can hear that philosophy all over this record. Compared to Uncontrollable Thoughts, The Sky Was Out of Tune is more dissolved. The previous album still had recognizable individual pieces—”Bird Song,” “Rainbow Road,” soft beats, organ drones, clear rhythmic personalities moving between tracks. Boundaries here have almost completely disappeared. Uncontrollable Thoughts felt like two musicians improvising compositions. This feels like those same two musicians improvising an environment. The rhythm is still present but behaves more like weather than percussion. Digital texture and ambience overlapping :: Soft electro rhythms surface throughout, especially when the album settles into its more defined sections. Nothing becomes overly forceful. Even when distortion enters it feels incorporated into the ambience rather than placed over it. There are moments that recall the softer edges of early Mille Plateaux material, digital texture and ambience overlapping until it becomes difficult to decide which one you’re actually listening to. The late 90s and early 2000s electronica sensibility is present throughout, that specific understanding that small rhythmic gestures can carry enormous emotional weight if given room. “VII” is the most interesting section on the record and it lasts 35 seconds. The glitches become more exposed, textures start colliding, and suddenly the album sounds like it might move somewhere completely different—like a corrupted transitional file that accidentally became part of the release. Its short duration is what gives it impact. “VII” functions as a doorway into “VIII” rather than a standalone piece. An introduction to the outro. And that tiny moment reveals something about the whole record, Chkheidze and Lippok are comfortable letting an idea exist only as long as it needs to. A texture doesn’t have to develop into a full track. A rhythmic pattern can appear for seconds and disappear. Something can sound important and still never return. The title describes the music unusually well. A sky being out of tune doesn’t mean the environment has collapsed, it means something familiar has shifted slightly enough that you start paying closer attention. That’s what happens here. Natural recordings, soft rhythms, distortion, metallic noises, melody, and digital artifacts continually lean against one another without settling. By the end it feels less like eight compositions and more like half an hour spent inside a system that was continuously adjusting itself while you were listening, and never quite finished. The Sky Was Out of Tune is available on Morr Music. [Bandcamp] The Sky Was Out of Tune by Anushka Chkheidze + Robert LippokThe post Anushka Chkheidze + Robert Lippok :: The Sky Was Out of Tune (Morr Music) first appeared on Igloo Magazine.
items._genre: ambient / glitch / experimental electronic / field recording
items._cn_summary: 这张专辑由格鲁吉亚作曲家/制作人Chkheidze与柏林电子老将Lippok合作，基于柏林Neue Nationalgalerie的现场演出发展而来。八首作品以罗马数字命名，更像是一个连续整体的多个段落而非独立曲目。自然录音、柔和节奏、失真、金属噪音、旋律与数字残响彼此依靠却从不落定。自然环境音作为准备铺垫，合成材料随后被推入其中，氛围逐渐积聚密度，失真缓慢浮现，微小节奏脉搏隐于表面再逐渐显现。两位音乐家擅长在揭示真正内容前引导听众预期——没有明显的段落切入或解决，所有变化都朝纹理迁移的方向推进。制作过程涉及长时间即兴、后期筛选创意、彼此互发工程文件，Chkheidze贡献鼓、钢琴、人声，Lippok加入电子层次。Morr Music作为承载电子、氛围、简约作曲交汇空间的老牌厂牌，为这种合作提供了自然归宿。

items.album: [2View] Maps and Diagrams’ beneath still stars (handstitched*) & returning light (Home Normal)
items.excerpt: Two decades removed from the clockwork IDM of Polytuft-Tech, Tim Martin’s returning light (Home Normal) and beneath still stars (handstitched*) find him stripping everything back to drift, texture, and quietly resonant melody, resulting in two companion albums that feel less like separate releases than different sides of the same long, unhurried thought.   Companion pieces, two sides of the same drift beneath still stars by maps and diagrams returning light by maps and diagrams   Tim M
items.body: Two decades removed from the clockwork IDM of Polytuft-Tech, Tim Martin’s returning light (Home Normal) and beneath still stars (handstitched*) find him stripping everything back to drift, texture, and quietly resonant melody, resulting in two companion albums that feel less like separate releases than different sides of the same long, unhurried thought.   Companion pieces, two sides of the same drift beneath still stars by maps and diagrams returning light by maps and diagrams   Tim Martin has been Maps and Diagrams since the early 2000s, and the entry point for a lot of people into his catalog is Polytuft-Tech, released in 2003 on Expanding Records, an album that got filed under IDM, ambient, and glitch at a moment when those three words together still meant something specific and rigorous. That record ran on clicky drums that whirred like clockwork under warm, streamlined melodies. It landed near the tail end of IDM’s most experimentally saturated period, right as the genre itself was quietly transitioning into whatever came next, and it stands as one of the more melodically generous statements from that stretch. Both returning light (Home Normal) and beneath still stars (handstitched*) are nowhere near that record sonically. Drums are gone almost entirely. Glitch has been replaced by drift. But it’s still unmistakably Tim, the same restrained, resonant signature that’s followed him through two decades of output, just aged into something quieter. Both albums arrive within weeks of each other on different labels with different histories attached. returning light is Home Normal‘s second release from Tim this year, following tone isolation, his actual debut on the label despite Home Normal running for over seventeen years, a gap explained by the fact that Tim‘s earliest UK work went through Nomadic Kids Republic, Home Normal‘s sister label, back in 2011 with Lights Will Call On You and The Town Beneath The Sea. beneath still stars comes out on handstitched*, the label Tim runs himself, which has carried his more private and experimental output for years alongside releases like In Circles. One album through someone else’s curatorial lens, one through his own. That distinction matters more than it initially seems to. Ambient releases should never get judged track by track in isolation. The genre works as a collective experience, an album like this either builds a sustained emotional environment across its runtime or it doesn’t, and no individual piece can really save or sink that outcome on its own. What matters more is whether the melodies that surface actually resonate, whether they invoke something specific rather than just occupying space. Both of these records succeed at that, though they do it through slightly different means. “ArcWorld-6.4 Rev.42 [sgl.break]” from beneath still stars is one of the more fascinating pieces across either release, another example of the part A / part B structure that’s shown up in other reviews recently. It connects two ideas without part B ever feeling like a continuation of part A. Instead it functions as an introduction to something entirely different, and the transition is peaceful in a way that most of this album is. The track titles throughout beneath still stars read almost like technical drafts, numbered revisions, hertz values, file extensions in brackets like [static] or [lost.wav] or [mem.void]. That naming isn’t arbitrary. It reads like an iteration system, drafts selected and refined specifically rather than titled decoratively after the fact. “Raddius.ocean-IX [r.36-04hz]” is another two-part piece, but this one connects rather than diverges, a drone-like melodic note giving way to a dreamlike synth tuned to a specific frequency, which the title tells you outright. Intentional down to the hertz. “beneath still stars and returning light aren’t competing statements, they’re companion pieces, two sides of the same drift, released close enough together that they start to feel like one long, unhurried thought that just happened to get split across two labels.” ~J. Batista A different level of drone entirely :: returning light sits in the same emotional register but sounds noticeably different sonically. There are small clicks and glitches scattered through certain tracks, and the pads and atmospheres carry a different weight than what’s happening on beneath still stars. “falling rainbows” uses static hits inside its pad environments to create reverbed textures that read almost like snare hits, except Tim‘s building that rhythmic tension entirely out of pad effects and reverb rather than anything resembling a drum sample. “just moving” introduces keys that sound almost like distortion at first before resolving into something prettier the longer you sit with it, a different level of drone entirely, since nothing here holds on a single note. There’s room for other melodies to form and enter, and they do. “somewhat virtual interactions” is a favorite, what sounds like a distorted “ahhh” vocal fragment sits so subtly in the mix that it changes the character of the pads around it, and there are field recording glitches scattered throughout that open up real space inside the track. “Open Water” plays almost like an audio representation of a shishi-odoshi—that traditional Japanese bamboo water fountain that fills, tips, empties, and resets in a slow repeating cycle. Tim‘s using effects here the same way that device uses gravity and water, building a soft, cyclical sense of rhythm entirely out of texture rather than percussion. “ouvertures” closes the album starting soft and distorted, and around the 3:55 mark a low humming frequency starts creeping in that sounds baked into the synth itself, eventually rolling and degrading the audio as the track winds down. A genuinely cool effect to end on. “Tim Martin has landed somewhere his younger self probably wasn’t building toward. Whether that’s evolution or just where two decades of making ambient music eventually deposits a person is hard to say, and probably doesn’t matter.” ~J. Batista There’s a version of this review that picks a favorite between the two records. That version would be missing the point entirely. beneath still stars and returning light aren’t competing statements, they’re companion pieces, two sides of the same drift, released close enough together that they start to feel like one long, unhurried thought that just happened to get split across two labels. beneath still stars is the more clinical of the pair. Drafted, revised, numbered like lab notes, every track title reading like a version history for a synth that never stops evolving. Twenty years removed from Polytuft-Tech‘s clockwork drums and whirring percussion, Tim Martin has landed somewhere his younger self probably wasn’t building toward. Whether that’s evolution or just where two decades of making ambient music eventually deposits a person is hard to say, and probably doesn’t matter. These two records don’t argue for themselves. They don’t need to. They just sit there, patiently, until you notice forty minutes have passed and you’ve barely moved. Home Normal got the warmer half. handstitched*—Tim‘s own label, his own house, got the rawer, more exacting one. He gets to have it both ways. So does anyone who sits with both records long enough to stop telling them apart. beneath still stars is available on handstitched* and returing light is available on Home Normal. beneath still stars by maps and diagrams returning light by maps and diagramsThe post [2View] Maps and Diagrams’ beneath still stars (handstitched*) & returning light (Home Normal) first appeared on Igloo Magazine.
items._cn_summary: Tim Martin以Maps and Diagrams之名活跃二十余年，早期以Polytuft-Tech的精密IDM闻名，而这两张专辑则彻底剥离鼓机与故障元素，转向纯粹的drift、texture与内敛旋律。returning light由Home Normal发行，beneath still stars则出自他自己经营的handstitched*厂牌，两者在不同策展视角下形成互补。评论强调氛围音乐应以整张专辑的持续情感场域来评判，而非逐曲拆解，认为这两张作品都成功构建了这种环境，使浮现的旋律具有真正的共鸣感，而非仅占据空间。文章未及完结，但从已呈现部分可看出，作者将这两张专辑视为同一漫长思绪的两面，是Tim Martin二十余年创作脉络中沉淀下来的安静篇章。

items.body: Review by Logan — Looking Beyond The Beautiful Space Out in the CountryThe short-form record tends to work on a different logic than a full LP. I value EPs that carry their own weight as intentional, self-contained pieces rather than just acting as a way to repackage existing music for sale.Much like a short film, an EP can use its brevity to settle into a specific mood or texture, without needing to extend those ideas across the length of a full studio album.Godspeed You Black Emperor!'s Slow Riot for New Zero Kanada does this well, letting tracks like "Moya" and "BBF3" create a heavy and distinct presence in under thirty minutes. Boards of Canada seems to approach the format similarly. A record like In a Beautiful Place Out in the Country does not feel like leftover tracks -- it works as an independent soundscape where the brief runtime is used for deliberate atmosphere.An important aspect of In a Beautiful Place Out in the Country is that these tracks do not appear on other major releases, which makes the EP an essential piece of their discography rather than a minor supplement. It stands out as one of my very favourite EPs. Listening to it highlights a beautiful and mysterious ambient density built on a sort of melancholy, discomforting and comforting nostalgia.I especially adore the tracks "Kid for Today" and "In a Beautiful Place Out in the Country" but I think the whole record is superb taken as a whole. "Zoetrope" did not at first appeal much, but during consecutive listens I got how its minimalist ambience worked with and added to the rest of the release. It helps to demonstrate how their use of repetitive, cyclical structures can reveal deeper qualities when one sits with the textures over a period of time. That highlights to me how a track can reward patience.I give it 5 stars as one of my most essential EPs.
items._cn_summary: 这张EP以极简的循环结构与重复音型构建出一种独特的氛围密度，介于怀旧与不安之间，带有忧郁而温暖的质感。Boards of Canada将电子采样的颗粒感与模拟合成器的朦胧质地相融合，营造出类似短片般的封闭空间感——短暂却完整。评论特别指出《Kid for Today》和《In a Beautiful Place Out in the Country》两首曲目为核心亮点，而最初不被看好的《Zoetrope》在反复聆听后展现出极简氛围如何服务于整体结构。这种需要耐心沉浸的聆听方式揭示了循环重复手法在电子音乐中的深层表现力，使整张EP成为独立且不可或缺的声音作品。

items.body: Review by Fercandio46 — When I first heard a few tracks by this Finnish band, I gradually realized that what captivated me was the blend of King Gizzard & The Lizard Wizard's irreverence toward musical genres, an approach that, while experimenting with them all, still respects them and follows their rules. I was also reminded of The Cardigans: a mix of tradition and the past, combined with a freshness where technology, jazz, and a unique brand of pop came together. Their debut album opens on a serious note with classical piano and violins, key elements of their sound, and the magical voice of Eeva Rajakangas; on the track "T�nne saakka ei aurinko paista," she recites the lyrics, creating a powerful and truly special moment. Kadenssi reveals the strong influence of Nordic traditional music, austere, profound, and almost sacred, and Celtic music, danceable and luminous, sharing a common thread in that both border on the mystical.With the fourth track, Kahdeksas p�iv�, rock and modernity enter the mix, while maintaining that distinctive nine-piece lineup, featuring two violins and a saxophone, where the true fusion begins. A folk atmosphere, driven by the flute, occasionally evokes the folk-rock sound of Jethro Tull; yet, modern drum loops and Eeva's spoken-word vocals merge into a blend of jazz, funk, and punk. Add to this a dissonant chorus and a distorted, psychedelic cabaret vibe, and it feels as though we are witnessing a whole new album within the album itself."Planeetta" plays with space and silence; Eeva's voice sings and then recedes, as does the piano, eventually revealing a jazz-infused atmosphere driven by violins and saxophone, lending the track a distinctive character. It then returns to Celtic roots, yet approaches them not in the traditional manner, but with a rock and funk sensibility, featuring a syncopated, irregular rhythm."08" continues with the distinctly postmodern vibe created by Eeva's spoken vocals, almost prophetic in tone, which has become a signature, recognizable style for the band. Just as Pessi Jouste's classical training is evident in the violin work, Aino Kallio's influence shines through on the piano; at times, the music evokes the atmosphere of chamber music, at others, Eastern and jazz styles reminiscent of Hiromi Uehara, or even the experimental approach of Alain Rochette (from the band Present). When the sound grows heavier, it becomes dense and dark, yet the strings and Eeva Rajakangas are always there, ensuring we never quite plunge over the precipice."Tarina" ventures into new territory; while Eeva sings and phrases with great freedom, she does so in tandem with a band that evokes the anarchic melodies of the Lounge Lizards, until the violins launch into a sort of tango reminiscent of the track "Palmiers En Pots" by the Belgian group Aksak Maboul. It is not even far-fetched to draw parallels with the Rock in Opposition scene; one can even detect traces of the early, defiant Bj�rk, alongside the bass-clarinet blues of Jaakko Arola."Vesi" evokes a violin-infused cabaret sung by Ute Lemper, yet the arrangements steer the sound toward danceable rhythms infused with punk currents, waves that surge in and recede. The band adapts perfectly to this variety of styles, skillfully navigating the challenge of maintaining overall cohesion. They stand as an impenetrable, unbreakable shield, much like the Baltic Shield, reflecting that Nordic light which lasts for months; a duration that pales in comparison to the enduring scope of their musical and artistic vision.

items._cn_summary: VIMMA的处作专辑将北欧传统民谣、凯尔特旋律与室内乐编制融为一体，九人编制涵盖双小提琴、萨克斯、钢琴与长笛。Eeva Rajakangas的人声穿梭于歌唱与念白之间，赋予作品近乎预言式的后现代质感。评论中提到的Lounge Lizards式无政府主义旋律、Ak sak Maboul式的探戈段落以及Hiromi Uehara般的爵士气质，使专辑在传统框架内持续向实验领域推进。摇滚与电子鼓loop的介入打破了民谣的抒情惯性，扭曲的psychedelic cabaret段落形成了专辑内部的自我更新。整体定位介于前卫民谣与RIO场景之间，呈现出一支九人乐队在严肃古典根基上展开跨界探索的野心与执行力。

items.excerpt: The ID:UD Senior Staff will spare no expense and forsake no opportunity to check out shows related to Our Thing and report back to you, the concerned and engaged reader and listener. Alex headed out to Toronto for the weekend in order to finally see the oft-promised, never delivered (until now) miracle of a live Tear Garden set, while Bruce stayed closer to home and checked out the Vancouver instalment of the Immortalis tour, featuring Past Self, Pink Stiletto, ET, Ringinger, and Covert Forces.
items.body: The ID:UD Senior Staff will spare no expense and forsake no opportunity to check out shows related to Our Thing and report back to you, the concerned and engaged reader and listener. Alex headed out to Toronto for the weekend in order to finally see the oft-promised, never delivered (until now) miracle of a live Tear Garden set, while Bruce stayed closer to home and checked out the Vancouver instalment of the Immortalis tour, featuring Past Self, Pink Stiletto, ET, Ringinger, and Covert Forces. We’ll have a full discussion of both nights on this week’s podcast. Okay, admittedly these are shows we’d still be going to even if we didn’t run a website and podcast dedicated to this biz, but we might as well make a meal of it, no? On with this week’s tracks. The Sick Man Of Europe Statiqbloom, “A Grief Observed” Votive, the latest three-track release from now veteran electro-industrial cum dark techno project Statiqbloom does a nice job of triangulating most of the sounds Fade Kainer’s employed under that name over the past decade, from murky half-time power electronics on “Cut The Vine” to more straightforward distorted kicks on “Erased”. But despite its very brief run-time, it’s the sickly acidic programming of “A Grief Observed”, crawling beneath Kainer’s mutters which is reminding us of why we’ve loved his psychedelic approach to vintage post-industrial for so long. Votive by Statiqbloom The Sick Man of Europe, “Apathy” Some pleasingly minimal but still melodic synth action from the UK’s Sick Man of Europe sure is hitting the spot right now. Maybe it’s the insistent drum programming, or the beleeping bass and synthwork, or the punky feedback on the lead, but the contrast between those elements and the frustration and anger of the lyrics certainly gives this one some juice. The Intermittent Signal by The Sick Man Of Europe Nick Viola, “Soft Brutalism” Nick Viola’s name should ring a bell to regular readers, either for his excellent work as Fractured Transmission or his role in the defunct Death Camp Audio clique releases from about a decade back (or his role in US supergroup HexRx, going back further), but a new EP under his own name functions as a good reintroduction to the read on dark techno he’s been working on in recent years. Dense and icy washes of distortion keep the kicks from ever running riot and pushing the subtler cyber programming out of the frame. Soft Brutalism by Nick Viola ᚾᛟᚢ, “Break Like Frost” Nothing Nordvargr finds while digging into his archives is likely to be “pleasant” in any traditional sense of the word. But it’s interesting to hear something like this pulled from the vaults, the first (so far as we can determine) release under the “ᚾᛟᚢ” name, clarifying the nominative distinction between Nordvargr and Trepaneringsritualen’s Thomas Martin Ekelund in their collaborative ᚾᛟᚢ II // ᚦᛟᚦ ᚷᛁᚷ project. Regardless of name or origin the icy mood of this piece’s drifts of death industrial and dark ambient soundscapes are apparent from the moment it begins even without looking at its title, with some classic lo-fi cassette style recording. Trollkorset by ᚾᛟᚢ Then Comes Silence, “Remaker Redeemer” Sweden’s Then Comes Silence make the kind of muscly, synth-inflected goth rock that has never truly gone out of style in Europe. And to their credit, they do it well; where so many acts who attempt the style have neither the vocal charisma nor the hooks to pull it off, TCS has plenty of both to spare. “Remaker Redeemer” has all kinds of mood and atmosphere, but doesn’t skimp on a big jump up chorus, accented by some grindy basswork and syncopated drums that make it fit for the club or the headphones. Requiem Ballroom by THEN COMES SILENCE Ye Gods, “Outlier (single edit)” Oh, to live in a world where songs like Ye Gods’ “Outlier” could be actual radio play singles. Kidding aside, we’re obviously huge fans of Antoni Maiovvi’s work, especially in the sprawling and conceptual esoteric canvas that the producer has made of Ye Gods (hear our interview from last year here), and this cut is no exception. It’s rhythmic, weird, lovely and unnerving, and often both at the same time. New EP Los comes out mid-October, mark it on your halloween calendars. Los by Ye Gods The post Tracks: October 5th, 2027 appeared first on I Die: You Die.

items._cn_summary: 这期乐评以多首曲目推荐的形式展开，聚焦于地下电子与后工业场景的近期作品。Statiqbloom的新作兼顾半速power electronics与失真底鼓，酸涩的编程与人声低语构成核心张力，延续其十年来的迷幻后工业路径。The Sick Man of Europe带来极简旋律化的合成器段落，鼓机驱动与合成器旋律线之间形成层次，歌词愤怒与器乐构成反差对比。Nick Viola的EP呈现冰冷密集的失真音景，抑制底鼓以突出细微的赛博编程细节，展现其对黑暗techno的独到理解。Nordvargr从档案中释出的ᚾᛟᚢ名义作品则在不愉悦的质地中呈现北欧地下场景的差异性定位，文章亦提及多场相关现场演出作为社群观察的延伸。

items.body: The reason I like John Coltrane’s Concert in Japan best out of all my Coltrane albums is that it includes one of my all-time favorite tracks: “Peace on Earth”. And as good as “Meditation/Leo (Part One),” “Leo (Part Two),” and “Part Three” are - “Peace on Earth” outshines them all. When John Coltrane arrived in Japan in 1966, he was welcomed like a king. He arrived at Haneda Airport on July 8, 1966, along with his wife Alice, Pharoah Sanders, Jimmy Garrison, and Rashied Ali. Ali, who later recalled the trip, said they were greeted by thousands of Japanese fans. At the airport, there were huge, life-size cardboard cutouts of the musicians, a red carpet leading from the plane to the terminal, and bouquets of flowers. And Coltrane had a message, it was no coincidence that he wanted to perform in Japan. He insisted on traveling to Nagasaki to visit the Peace Memorial at the site of the atomic bombing. He laid down a wreath and prayed for a long time. The place had a profound emotional and spiritual impact on him. On the evening of his concert in Nagasaki, he played “Peace on Earth” - at that time a new piece and a kind of musical prayer for peace. At a press conference during the tour, when asked about the Vietnam War, he said: “I dislike war, period. It should stop, and any other war.” On Concert in Japan - and on “Peace on Earth” in particular - one can see how Coltrane’s thirst for new sounds is inextricably linked to his desire to view the universe from a spiritual perspective; his music radiates a cosmic aura. The piece begins with an incredibly beautiful melody that floats above Alice’s arpeggios, Garrison’s bass sprinklings, and Ali’s sparse drumming. It seems like the musical embodiment of the Garden of Eden. Nearly six minutes of pure harmony - but then deliberate atonality creeps in, paradise is threatened, only heavenly saxophone lines save it for the time being. Then, however, a dissonant storm is conjured up, shaking this world to its very foundations. The piece is thrown into utter disarray; block chords replace the arpeggios, and the bass and drums throw the meter overboard. At the very end, however, harmony returns, and the melodies resurface, albeit different from how they began. In July 1966, John Coltrane was just one year away from his untimely death, yet his zest for life was greater than ever. His musical explorations were more adventurous than before, and “Peace on Earth” brilliantly captures the essence of what his music is all about. Or, as my friend Thomas Weber puts it: “On the one hand, it’s utter extravagance and exhaustion, on the other, it’s the dissolution of boundaries. Free jazz with melodies.” Email This BlogThis! Share to X Share to Facebook
items._cn_summary: 这张1966年日本现场录音聚焦Coltrane晚期最具实验性的创作之一《Peace on Earth》。评论追溯了他前往长崎和平纪念碑献花的历史背景，使这首作品成为以音乐祈求和平的精神宣言。演奏从近六分钟的纯净和谐展开，Alice Coltrane的琶音、Garrison的低音点缀与Ali稀疏的鼓击共同构筑天堂般的音响空间。随后有意识的无调性侵入，不协和的风暴将调性彻底颠覆，块状和弦取代琶音，节拍被抛弃。最终和声回归但旋律已面目全非。评论特别强调Coltrane对宇宙的精神性视角与对新声音的渴求如何在此作品中不可分割地交织，音乐散发出宇宙般的光晕。这是Coltrane逝世前一年所留下的最具冒险精神的音乐探索之一。

items.body: God Is Everything You Are Not is built from voice, MicroKORG synthesis, a microphonic soundbox from LeafAudio, and field recordings. Seven pieces, just under 36 minutes. The release notes describe grief approached as passage rather than narrative, and that framing holds, this record puts you inside the duration of something rather than telling you it happened. Voice-forward, inward-facing, unconcerned with visibility God Is Everything You Are Not by Elika Ostrov   Fort Evil Fruit is a small Irish imprint that consistently operates in spaces most labels avoid, quiet, uncomfortable, structurally unconventional work sitting between sound art and song. Elika Ostrov fits that context without friction. Outside of this release there’s very little information available on her, which feels appropriate given how the record presents itself: voice-forward, inward-facing, unconcerned with visibility. God Is Everything You Are Not is built from voice, MicroKORG synthesis, a microphonic soundbox from LeafAudio, and field recordings. Seven pieces, just under 36 minutes. The release notes describe grief approached as passage rather than narrative, and that framing holds, this record puts you inside the duration of something rather than telling you it happened. “Candy Apple Pie” opens things and it’s the track that pulled me in first. Her voice carries the whole weight of the piece, sitting on top of what sounds like lightly bitcrushed synth underneath. There’s something almost melodic about it, almost settled. One of the warmer moments on the record, which catches you off guard given what the album is called. From there things get quieter and darker. “Kapu” sustains that shift without forcing it—the synth texture recedes further into the background noise and the grief the album orbits starts to feel more present, less described. It doesn’t announce itself. None of these pieces follow any conventional structure. Rhythms don’t materialize. Nothing locks in. The whole thing sounds loosely assembled, and that’s the point, the album is designed to feel like something you’re moving through rather than observing. Background is the compositional choice, not a byproduct of it. The title track runs 16:45 and arrives at the end like a separate document entirely. Ringing ambience opens it, sustained long enough that it starts to accumulate into something disorienting. Running underneath that is a static interference noise, the exact frequency you’d get from a phone sitting too close to a receiver, that ticking electrical feedback. That specific texture generates most of the tension in the piece. Ostrov speaks throughout but the audio is reversed, her voice present and completely inaccessible at the same time. You hear her talking for the full duration without understanding a word. Then, toward the end, the audio flips forward and you can actually hear her. Sixteen minutes of building toward a moment it never telegraphed. That ticking electrical feedback :: The closest reference points for the record’s overall aesthetic are somewhere between the warped loop logic of Dat Politics, the peculiar stillness of Boards of Canada at their most unsettling, and the indie-adjacent vocal sensibility of Noriko Tujiko. Ostrov shares certain instincts with all three without directly resembling any of them. The reverse-to-forward reveal on the title track stays with you after the record ends. Grief made audible as a structural decision, not a theme. Experimental electronic music has always found its most interesting moments when artists stop treating it as a genre and start treating it as a method. The tools shift, tape gave way to DAWs, DAWs gave way to modular, modular gave way to whatever hybrid setups artists are running now, but the impulse underneath stays the same. Find a way to make the listener feel something the conventional song structure can’t reach. Ostrov is working in that tradition without announcing it. The MicroKORG and the LeafAudio soundbox and the reversed vocals aren’t chosen for their novelty. They’re chosen because they do specific things to time and memory and presence that a guitar and a verse-chorus wouldn’t. That’s what keeps this corner of music alive, artists who use the tools as extensions of the idea rather than the idea itself. God Is Everything You Are Not is exactly that kind of record. God Is Everything You Are Not is available on Fort Evil Fruit. items._cn_summary: 这张专辑由人声、MicroKORG合成器、LeafAudio麦克风声箱以及田野录音构建而成，共七首作品，总时长约36分钟。整张作品以声音艺术的手法处理哀悼这一主题，不提供叙事而是让听者置身于时间的流逝之中。开场曲以人声为绝对主导，合成器仅作为隐约的铺垫，随后整体走向逐渐沉入更暗、更安静的质地。标题曲目占据专辑最后16分45秒，以持续铃声质感开场，配合类似电话干扰的静态电流噪音制造张力，整首作品中演唱者的声音被反转处理，十六分钟里你只能听到她在说话却无法理解任何一个字，直到尾声声音才被翻转为正向。整张专辑没有传统曲式、没有节奏支撑、没有可预期的结构，背景噪音本身就是作曲的选择，声音的组织方式是松散的，目的是让听者感觉自己正在穿过某个过程而非旁观某个事件。

items.body: wave_function ultimately displays an artist working in top form, mapping out a series of experimental electronic terrains that converge into something uniformly disjointed, immersive, and quietly mind-bending. Broken sonic relics, elastic and stretched to their limits wave_function by Marco Simioni   One of our favorite mechanized glitch-electronic artists, Marco Simioni, returns with wave_function for Barcelona-based Evel, an imprint that continues pushing fractured, futuristic sound-scrapes from artists across the planet. Simioni digs miles and miles into erratic, densely packed rhythmic DSP-laden structures, shaping minimalist extrusions that echo, bend, and arch. Opener “et II no pt re” feels as though its pulsing tone and abrasive grit could push straight through the cosmos. Corrupted sonic data, indeed. Simioni works in infinitesimal layers, carefully weaving hypnotic electro-glitch hybrids into shifting forms and textures. Tracks like “yttr flux” and “vinh 49” emerge as broken sonic relics, elastic and stretched to their limits, while “pulse array for dissolving realities (dive mix)” moves through a restrained ambient propulsion, industrial drone filaments threading through the mix like fragments of an unknown message waiting to be deciphered. “ekkot vire” pushes deeper into abstract electronic substructures, constantly expanding, collapsing, and reforming, before “509dualech2211eren” loops through a haze of ambient flutter, surrounding the listener with microscopic details of tone, drone, and white noise. The ending highlights Simioni’s ability to cultivate tiny, ethereal sound forms that remain ruptured at their edges while maintaining the pulse of a living machine. wave_function ultimately displays an artist working in top form, mapping out a series of experimental electronic terrains that converge into something uniformly disjointed, immersive, and quietly mind-bending. elseq fans should take immediate notice. wave_function is available on Evel. items._cn_summary: 这是一张以故障电子与工业嗡鸣为核心的实验专辑，艺术家通过微观层面的层次编织，将极简主义声响拉伸、扭曲并重组。曲目在抽象电子子结构中不断展开、崩塌与重塑：开场曲以脉冲音与粗糙颗粒感贯穿宇宙感，后续曲目以破碎的声响遗骸呈现弹性极限，而中段作品则在环境推进力中嵌入工业嗡鸣丝线，仿佛等待破译的密码碎片。整张专辑构建出一系列实验电子地形，最终汇聚为统一而割裂的沉浸式听觉体验。评论明确指出这是艺术家最佳状态的呈现，并向爱好者发出强烈推荐信号。

items.body: A mesmerizing collision of ambient, jazz, electronics and ritualistic textures, this album unfolds like a deep-space journey that never loses its human pulse. Trumpet drifts through electronic vastness Fade In Brighter Age by Pulsar + Demetrio Cecchitelli   Mahorka has a busy schedule and quite an enormous back catalog, covering various electronic music, from ambient to dub, noise and radically experimental. Confirmed sound artists meet new promising ones in the course of indie, challenging music with no regard for major commercial tendencies. I’ve never heard of Pulsar (Leonardo Pucci) before, but I must say he perfectly teams up with Demitrio Cecchitelli. I’m more familiar with the work of Cecchitelli, notably with the sumptuous Empetus (published years ago by Midira). The addition of trumpet player Jacopo Buda to the soundscapes gives an enriched musical meaning to the album, playing the card of instrumental ambient music with partly experimental-jazzy tones and expansive improvs which evolve on dynamic electronic textures. What we can listen to here is nothing less than a furiously enthralling and original musical trip which starts masterfully with the ethno-ritual and spaced-out “Cosmic Dream”. Such a gorgeous piece with its perpetual circular rhythms covered by inspiring and gently minimal trumpet melodic shifts. It is meticulously crafted without being purely ambient, as it conjugates a vast array of influences, from Buddhist-Zen musical attributes to early minimalism and atmospheric, then bassy, chilled-out vibes. It suggests immensity and nature-like vastness, with its colorful timbres resonating in divine harmony. It is a sprawling track with a magnificent development, always suspenseful, melodically ethereal and dynamic. The second track (“Expanding Light”) also operates a nice syncretism and musical dialogue between acoustic ingredients, wind instruments and electronics, but here we enter a more downtempo, softly moving ambience, less lyrical and tripped-out but equally good and perfectly elaborated. The title track (“Fade in Brighter Age”) almost provides a softly moving dream-pop quality, built on guitars, vibrant chords and slowly enveloping wind sequences, largely embracing a lonesome path and a feeling of consciousness at night. All in all, a varied and semi-jazzy atmospheric ambient album with a flowing cinematic edge. Absolutely recommended and easily one of my personal favorites of this year. For fans of John Hassell, Harold Budd, Peter Knight, Loscil, Bersanin Quartett, Nala Sinephro, and Floating Points. Fade In Brighter Age is available on Mahorka. items.body: On Orthodox Tapes, London-based artist Andrew Sherwell dives into the dusty vortex of the past, using the style of hauntology to pursue a place of personal recollection and warm remembrance. Hauntology doesn’t usually highlight warmth. The Caretaker uses it to examine the horrifying decline of the mind while Pye Corner Audio uses it as a kind of ghost-box through which spirits and cool, VHS-recorded synths enter; it’s a style reeking of decay. Orthodox Tapes runs close to the latter because it broadcasts not only the music of the past but a life of the past. In this instance, nocturnal tape loops and creased-up field recordings summon up the many experiences of Andrew’s grandfather, who once travelled back and forth through the Balkans, Central Europe and Southern Russia during the inter-war period. Andrew would spend school holidays at his grandfather’s house, where, as an old man, he would recount his many adventures over a bedtime story. The evening light fused with deep recollections and fantastical tales of bygone days: encounters with local people and their folk tales, stories of Orthodox bishops and beautiful princesses, of demons lurking in pure daylight and angels in human form, of days spent in endless forests and nights camped out on the grasslands, staring up at the bright silver moon and the sequined stars. Needless to say, these stories had a powerful impact on Andrew as a child, and the music is equally mysterious, sprinkled in memory-dust, bewitching the listener with its world of ambient sighs, dim crackles and dusty echoes. The projector starts up, whirring away in the background as a ghostly chorus appears, slowly drawing the listener deeper and deeper into its past life. Church bells clank in an old town, and vapours rise out of the slumbering world. Orthodox Tapes slinks away from reality, descending into the deep pools of sleep. Mermaids are masqueraded in a curdled pool of unclear water and fantastical things swim underneath. This isn’t the real world – it’s something better. It’s a place of tranquil escape. These voices lie on the pillow-soft clouds of a beautiful (if strange) dream. Because of his personal connection, love seeps out of the music, giving the airy atmosphere a romanticized vibe: it’s the scent of old times and of unbreakable ties, of comfort and deep familiarity…and of ultimate rest. But this was a tumultuous time – some believed it to be the end of days – and the drones slip into foggy voids, too. ‘Beware Koschei’s Visit’ is one example of the mood’s relegation, and that’s how the record ends, expressing both sides of the story: the narrator and the listener, the artist and the audience…the magic of childhood, oblivious to a frightening world on the other side of that bedroom door and the untold horrors across the sea. www.whitelabrecs.bandcamp.com
items._genre: hauntology / ambient / field recording / drone / experimental
items._cn_summary: 伦敦艺术家Andrew Sherwell 以hauntology为框架，将祖父在战间期穿越巴尔干、中欧与南俄的回忆转化为声音文本。作品以夜间的磁带循环、皱褶般的田野录音与朦胧的回响构成叙事通道：教堂钟声在古镇中敲响，雾气自沉睡的世界升起，独白漂浮在枕畔般柔软的云层之上。乐评指出音乐同时映射了双重视角——童话般的安全梦境与门外动荡世界之间的对照，末曲以低沉嗡鸣暗示Koschei来访的险恶征兆。整张专辑从私人情感出发，将东欧民间传说与录音艺术融合，散发浓郁的怀旧气息和家族记忆的温度，是对消失世界的声音档案化重建，体现出独立厂牌难得的艺术深度。

items.body: Matt Carlson is one half of Portland, Oregon duo Golden Retriever, and has also released a number of solo recordings under his own name. His latest, for French label Shelter Press, demonstrates his interest in linguistics and language games, combining heavily processed and manipulated voices with blooping and chirping modular synthesis. Sometimes the voices are squeezed to the point of wordlessness, simply pitched tones that are never quite simply pitched tones because of their still-recognisable source in human speech. At other times, such as in the tracks “The Game” and “An Enhanced Interrogation of Authenticity”, the meanings of words and their modes of presentation are played with to dizzying and disorienting effect. In some ways, “The View From Nowhere” reminds me of the work of US artist Bruce Nauman, particularly his classic video works such as “Good Boy Bad Boy” and “Clown Torture”. In these works, Nauman uses repetition, recontextualisation, and similar techniques to transform language into sculpture-like objects, revealing its inherent absurdity and arbitrariness. The same devices are frequently used by Carlson, but while Nauman was primarily concerned with critiquing the use of language to exercise power and inflict violence, the Portlander seems genuinely interested in the intricacies of linguistic science and the ways in which, through repetition and social injunction, the meanings of language gestures come to be attributed or undermined. The synthesised elements of the album reflect this theme, with rapid-fire pulses, sweeping filters and pans, and shimmering textures mirroring the complex and constantly shifting sands of verbal discourse. The vocal sounds mingle freely with the instrumental ones, being multiplied, echoed, and filtered to the point where they often become rhythmic and tonal elements in themselves. While genuine in its attempts to engage in a musical way with linguistic theory, “The View From Nowhere” retains Nauman’s penchant for the absurd and for off-kilter humour, turning what could have been quite a dry, impenetrable exercise into something intriguing and fun.   The View From Nowhere by Matt Carlson   Matt Carlson Shelter Press
items._genre: experimental electronic / vocal manipulation / modular synthesis
items._cn_summary: 这张专辑将人声作为核心素材，通过深度处理与模块化合成器相结合，探索语言学的复杂性。作者将人声挤压至丧失词义的纯音调状态，同时保留可辨识的人类语音来源特质，营造出眩晕而迷失方向的听感。专辑让人联想到Bruce Nauman的影像作品——通过重复与语境重构，将语言转化为雕塑般的对象，揭示其内在的荒谬与任意性。合成器元素中快速脉冲、扫频滤波与闪烁质感映射着话语不断流动的复杂地形。人声与器乐声音自由融合、互相渗透，经常转化为节奏与音调元素本身。专辑以音乐方式认真探讨语言理论，同时保留了荒诞与怪趣的幽默感，将本可能枯燥的学术练习转化为引人入胜且充满趣味的聆听体验。

items.body: Lines The Polish clarinetist and composer Waclaw Zimpel has played in numerous bands over the years, including, most recently, his own Waclaw Zimpel Quartet, and the Waclaw Zimpel To Tu Orchestra, with which he released the notable albums Stone Fog (2013) and Nature Moves (2014) respectively, on the excellent jazz label For Tune. Lines is his first solo effort. “What I had in mind was mostly polyphonic music but I couldn’t see a point in working on this with other players,” says Zimpel. “First of all, I wanted to perform most of the melodic lines on clarinets. I had a very precise vision of how those lines should be composed and it felt very natural to perform all of them by myself. Secondly, this album is mostly written not improvised so I had no problem recording track after track feeling that some of live-performance spontaneity is being lost,” he adds. Zimpel is something of a scholar. Over the years he’s delved into the musical traditions of India, Japan, and Morocco and researched the roots of improvisation from liturgical music to African trance. With Lines, the Polish clarinetist constructs an intricate sonic framework of parallel chords that attain a ritualistic effect by virtue of their varying configuration. He explores the depths of sound by unhinging any linearity in time that might carry a narrative intention in order to unveil new projections of aural space. Different musical environments are suggested, although the opening track, Alupa – Pappa, locates the album firmly in the Minimalist camp and sets the tone. “I think that you can sense this characteristic approach to space and sound is audible on all compositions, despite the fact that they differ between themselves. What might be the main common denominator is the inspiration I drew from the pioneers of American minimalism, like La Monte Young and Terry Riley. Some parts of ‘Lines’ are in a way a paraphrasis of their formal ideas from the 60’s and 70’s. I also believe that ‘Deo Gratias’, being a Renaissance canon in its own way, also fits this concept as a prophecy of minimalism composed 500 years earlier,” explains Waclaw. Notwithstanding the subtly shifting patterns of the album, it would be misleading to think, that Lines is just a modern take on Minimalism, even if the debt to Reich, Riley & co is undeniable, as the title track testifies. Moreover, the philological approach is guaranteed by the use of Hammond organ and fender Rhodes, which appear elsewhere in the album. Zimpel’s take, though, is wider in scope. As he mentions, with Deo Gratias he also looks back at the work of the Flemish 15th century singer, choirmaster, and composer Johannes Ockeghem. Zimpel mimics the density of events in Ockeghem’s polyphonic music, often giving each new voice he introduces throughout the album, something different to say about any melodic or rhythmic idea proposed by another. This is achieved in a remarkably unlabored and seemingly effortless manner. The emphasis is always on the emotional undercurrent that seeps through loops and tones. The organic quality of the sound is mesmerizing in its flow. The rhythmic spell is only eventually broken midway through the closing track Tak Picture, only to resurface briefly before finally grinding to a halt. Lines by Wac?aw Zimpel Lines is out on Instant Classics on February 5, 2016 A beautiful black and white video of Waclaw Zimpel performing lines can be seen here www.waclawzimpel.pl
items._cn_summary: 波兰单簧管演奏家兼作曲家Waclaw Zimpel的首张个人专辑《Lines》，以独奏形式呈现多声部复调构想。单簧管、Hammond风琴与Fender Rhodes电钢琴交织出平行和弦的仪式感声场，解构时间线性以拓展听觉空间。作品明显受美国极简主义先驱La Monte Young与Terry Riley影响，但并非简单复刻——标题曲与《Deo Gratias》等曲目回溯至15世纪弗兰德乐派复调传统，将Ockeghem的多声部密度转化为现代语境下的持续低音与相位叠加。每条旋律线各自独立又彼此对话，学者式的跨文化研究（印度、日本、摩洛哥音乐传统及从礼仪音乐到非洲出神仪式的即兴溯源）为专辑注入厚重的学术纵深。专辑放弃了即兴成分，以精确写作为骨架，在极简主义框架内探索音色层次与和声运动的微观变化，是一张兼具结构严谨性与冥想质感的独奏作品。

items.body: Palagoma is not only the first release from Nairobi-based label Cool Waters, it also marks the first time German-born, Kenya-based percussionist Sven Kacirek has collaborated with Ogoya Nengo and Olith Ratengo at the same time. Odd Okoddo, the duo of Kacirek and Ratengo, has been performing since 2018, but with the inclusion of the 83 year old Nengo, a singer from the eastern part of the country, there�s an added traditional depth to the music. A 2025 performance shows Nengo�s lifetime of experience singing Kenya�s dodo tradition around 2 and half minutes in (see below). Furthermore, her inclusion on this album allows her and Ratengo to toss the vocals back and forth as they reference their shared roots (Ratengo and Nengo live minutes from each other). Musically, however, the tracks are driven by Kacirek�s Buchla synth, hand percussion, and occasional kit drumming, which serve to buoy the voices without blotting out the music�s origins. Palagoma by Odd Okoddo & Ogoya Nengo �Bara,� for example, begins with the dime-store thwack of a repeated pattern, a stiff juxtaposition to the voices; yet, as the song rolls along, a 4/4 clink appears, then a burbling bass, and finally, what sounds like a xylophone. Layers of synthesized polyrhythms keep presenting themselves with a subtlety almost unnoticeable, until, by the track�s end, it feels organic, as if it�s all been underneath the two voices all along. Palagoma by Odd Okoddo & Ogoya Nengo �Sarah,� perhaps the album�s most intense track, features a lead vocal from Ratengo and tentative, percussive spittles from Kacirek. And while the technology never tries to overtake the vocals, it does sneak up and punctuate the track�s urgency, as edgy distortion sneaks in here and there just as Ratengo�s voice reaches its peak. The term �folktronica� has been bandied about as a way to house the type of music on offer here. In fact, exploratory collaborations such as Chouk Bwa & The �ngstr�mers as well as much of Kampala, Uganda�s Nyege Nyege label house sounds that might be �folktronic� in some way. What�s more interesting and important about this music, though, is how truly global so much of it is while maintaining a deep connection to Africa and its diasporic communities. The music on Palagoma , as well as much of what�s linked above (and available in countless other recent recordings) demonstrates a real willingness for cultures to respond to each other without trampling traditions altogether. Instead, roots become avant-garde and innovations become seemingly thousands of years old. Certainly the inclusion of an 83 year old traditional Kenyan singer only recently making her global debut as she tours with a duo whose instrumental voice is a white male saturated in electronic Kenyan rhythms demonstrates this blurring. The music this trio makes is certainly of the 21st century, but it�s often hazy, sparse, and open, keeping it from a quick sell-by date or confining it to a specific genre. Instead, it�s a beautiful example music as grace.

items._cn_summary: 这张专辑来自内罗毕新晋厂牌Cool Waters，由德国裔肯尼亚鼓手与两位当地音乐人合作完成，核心亮点在于将83岁传统肯尼亚dodo歌唱风格的资深女歌手纳入电子化框架。制作以Buchla合成器、手打击乐与电子节奏为底色，逐步叠加的复节奏层与即兴段落展现出鲜明的实验意识：合成器音色从廉价敲击感渐变为有机流动，人声始终居于前景而不被技术淹没。两位人声歌手因地域相近而形成天然呼应，传统对唱与电子脉冲之间构成持续张力。乐评将其与Nyege Nyege厂牌的非洲先锋电子场景并置，强调这类跨文化协作的全球化特质——传统未被覆盖，而是转化为前卫语汇。整体呈现出非洲根源与当代电子制作的双向融合，制作手法细腻且具层次感。

items.album: Francesco Paolo Paladino and Luca Chino Ferrari
items.artist: Dorothy Moskowitz & United States of Alchemy
items.excerpt:
Known for playing with County Joe McDonald, and for her experimental sound band The United States of America, Dorothy Moskowitz came back in 2023 with United States of Alchemy and their well-received release,
Under an Endless Sky
.
In collaboration with avant-garde composer and filmmaker Francesco Paolo Paladino, and poet and music writer Luca Chino Ferrari,
Songs of Compassion
is eleven songs containing subversive and at times beautiful music, and richly evocative lyrics.
Francesco Paolo Paladi
items.body: Known for playing with County Joe McDonald, and for her experimental sound band The United States of America, Dorothy Moskowitz came back in 2023 with United States of Alchemy and their well-received release, Under an Endless Sky . In collaboration with avant-garde composer and filmmaker Francesco Paolo Paladino, and poet and music writer Luca Chino Ferrari, Songs of Compassion is eleven songs containing subversive and at times beautiful music, and richly evocative lyrics. Francesco Paolo Paladino and Luca Chino Ferrari | Photo by Maria Assunta Karini Songs of Compassion has two challenges for the listener. The first is the music, called variously avant-garde, ambient, modal, non-linear, and a few more. It is played mostly on pianos mixed in and out of the foreground, sometimes doubled, and sometimes out of phase, joined by strings, woodwinds, synth washes, and steely sounds. Initially disorienting, the music serves to remind us how locked our minds are to Western notions of harmonic movement. It speaks of alternative musical narratives much older and much further away. They are songs that subvert the song: more like Steve Reich than Steve Stills; more like Phillip Glass than Phil Collins. UNITED STATES OF ALCHEMY - Pale Wanderer At the same time, there are the poetic yet strikingly contemporary lyrics. �Pale Wanderer� talks about the fact that authoritarianism needs willing accomplices, describing what happens �When you make a deal with darkness.� UNITED STATES OF ALCHEMY (Dorothy Moskowitz, Francesco Paolo Paladino e Luka Chino Ferrari) by Silentes �Charlottesville� (written with the late Joe Byrd) evokes the time not long ago when torch-wielding nazis, proud of the metaphoric Ns on their tunics, chanted the antisemitic tropes paraphrased in Moskowitz�s words, �We�ll be one people, pure of race/No greedy throng could take our place� . Besides the overtly political lyrics, in the tradition of 1960s protest songs, there are also thoughtful meditations on mortality and our place in the universe. The message is high-minded yet sincere and direct. World weary and wise, Moskowitz�s voice inhabits the evocative philosophical lyrics with the authority of a skilled method actor. The melodies unfold like streams of consciousness, rising and falling, not following expected diatonic chord progressions, but honouring, instead, the value of each word. Moskowitz�s piano acts as another voice and sometimes a kind of Greek chorus commenting on the proceedings. The surrounding music frames, creates pulses and dissonances, and shimmers. The return of Dorothy Moskowitz with her renamed project has arrived in a moment quite similar to the times that spawned its predecessor. Political division, unrest, and uncertainty always generate artistic reaction, and United States of Alchemy roared back to life with their epic 24-minute opening track �Under an Endless Sky� in 2023, serving perhaps as an �In-A-Gadda-Da-Vida� for our times. Songs of Compassion continues to challenge how we think about our world. It�s music that defies the song form, while doing exactly what music is supposed to do�enrich the human condition. Find the artist online. The title track from the 2023 U.S. of Alchemy recording Under an Endless Sky by Dorothy Moskowitz & United States of Alchemy Further reading Cris Derksen - The Visit (Review) Tiny Sun - Vanishment (Review) Maria Ka - Di Mashin (Review) Further listening You will find a number of Dorothy Moskowitz's works on Race The Sky , most recently on Podgrammes #022 and #019.
items.label: Songs of Compassion
items._genre: avant-garde / experimental / ambient / protest song / contemporary composition
items._cn_summary: Dorothy Moskowitz联合前卫作曲家Francesco Paolo Paladino与诗人Luca Chino Ferrari推出专辑《Songs of Compassion》，收录十一首作品。音乐以钢琴为核心，辅以弦乐、木管与合成器织体，采用非线性和调式手法，刻意打破西方和声进行的惯性思维，呈现接近Steve Reich与Philip Glass的极简复调美学。Moskowitz的演唱不循常规音阶，旋律随意识流动，每个词都被赋予独立分量。歌词延续六十年代抗议传统，从反对权威主义的政治批判到对死亡与宇宙位置的哲思，形成严肃而不迂腐的表达。整体在实验音乐框架内注入明确的政治与诗学意图，呈现出罕见的跨年代延续性。

items.body: Tako Toki are like desert island musicians who, castaway without their instruments, were forced to construct their own. Lucky for us, they are as skilled in making instruments as they are in creating original songs with which to show off their handicrafts. Un Dimanche � Monaco is the band�s follow-up to their well-received debut, Hirsute Farfelus , with a similar mash of musical styles. Before discussing the music, we need to talk about their instrument closet. They really have built everything they play out of bric-a-brac, odds and ends, and rubbish. I�m not sure from listening which is which, but they call their instruments, in an incomplete list, tassofons, tilofons, and tubofones, clarinuts, didjerimou, and klarbass, and my favorite, kitchenofon. (I will refer to what I hear by the names of store-bought instruments that they sound like.) The most surprising thing for me was how accurate the instruments were to pitch and how good they sounded under the harsh scrutiny of modern recording microphones that have documented a rich, high-quality sound. UN DIMANCHE A MONACO - LP by Tako Toki They have also very effectively matched their choice of instruments with the style of music that inspires their compositions. Right off the top, �Yinitza� features a laughing clarinet singing a klezmer tune accompanied by bassoon for the bass, frantic two-time percussion, and the exuberant human yelps found on many klezmer recordings. As on this track, many tunes feature improvisations that show an impressive degree of musicianship. On the cumbia-inspired �Le Cuenta,� the characteristic flute carries the tune, augmented by a Spanish singing chorus, and remarkably rich-sounding Latin percussion. The title track surrounds us with afrobeat woodblocks, shakers, and rattles scattered around the mix. The melody is played on a marimba ornamented with bells and cymbals. Again, the lead player improvises over the tune and often against the beat with jazzy chops. The flute returns on the samba-inspired �Ambiguidade,� and on �Aksum� it traces a trance-like Middle Eastern tune reminiscent of a 60s TV spy-show theme. UN DIMANCHE A MONACO - LP by Tako Toki Full of fun and one of a kind, Un Dimanche � Monaco celebrates our universal love of rhythmic, melodic, and harmonic sounds and the varied, wonderful ways cultures have organized that love in what we call music. At the same time, playing on literal pieces of junk, Tako Tiko reminds us, as we contemplate many mall music shops filled with gleaming wood and brass instruments and countless unused guitars lying in closets, that musicians will always find a way to make music. Find the artist online. Further reading: Tako Toki - Hirsute Farfelus (Review) Terje Isungset - Glacial Poetry (Review)

items._cn_summary: 这支乐队从废弃物和边角料中亲手制作所有乐器，包括自制的tassofons、tilofons、tubofones以及颇具趣味的kitchenofon等。这些自制乐器不仅音准准确，在高品质录音下依然展现出丰富饱满的音质。音乐风格横跨多元文化，'Yinitza'展现克莱兹默传统，笑声般的单簧管与巴松和疯狂打击乐交织；'Le Cuenta'融入昆比亚节奏，长笛与西班牙合唱团相伴；同名曲呈现非洲节拍元素，木鱼与沙锤散布混响中，旋律由马林巴琴演奏并辅以即兴爵士段落；'Ambiguidade'展现桑巴灵感，'Aksum'则带有中东迷幻色彩，长笛勾勒出类似六十年代间谍剧主题曲的氛围。整张专辑将世界音乐的多样性与自制乐器的实验精神相结合，呈现一场跨文化声音实验，同时提醒人们音乐的本质远胜于乐器的材质。

items.body: After the extra-terrestial explorations of Eventyrferd , the previous album from Norway's Camilla Hole Trio, in which sci-fi synth sounds were married with traditional material, their latest release Langs is rather more earthbound. But the quest to look beyond their own country's folk music continues. Camilla Hole's main instrument being the soprano sax, the influence of jazz is unsurprising and this is evident in the opening track �Springleik,� signifying a tune used to accompany the springleik dance from the west of Norway. Initially Hole takes the melody with Egil Kalman and Knut Kvifte Nesheim providing rhythmic support on double bass and drums respectively, with the overdubbing of Kalman's modular synth and Nesheim's vibraphone adding colour. But characteristically for this trio, in which assigned roles are never clearly defined or adhered to, things soon start to move around, with Kalman taking up the melody on his bass, playing the melody in unison with Hole, while Nesheim opens things out further rhythmically. As the whole piece takes on a much more improvisatory feel, Hole plays the melody one more time as things draw to a close. Langs by Camilla Hole Trio

items._cn_summary: 这张专辑是Camilla Hole Trio继《Eventyrferd》之后的最新作品，从前作的外太空式合成器探索转向更为脚踏实地的方向，但仍延续了对本国传统民间音乐的超越性追寻。主奏乐器为高音萨克斯，融合爵士即兴与挪威西部传统舞蹈音乐"Springleik"。乐队三人角色界限模糊，Kalman的低音提琴可承接旋律与萨克斯齐奏，Nesheim的鼓与颤音琴共同拓展节奏空间，模块化合成器叠合增添音色层次。整首曲目结构自由流动，从主题陈述逐渐过渡到开放式即兴，结尾再以旋律回归收束，体现了北欧爵士特有的冷静质感与传统素材的现代重构。

items.body: Sendas by Omar Sosa True to a Monk-inspired commitment never to play the same thing twice, Cuban pianist and composer Omar Sosa�s Sendas (Pathways), his latest solo offering, is the vivid invention of a pensive, restlessly creative, evolutionary artistry. As with all Sosa�s work, Sendas is the fortunate product of serendipity. In 2021 the COVID lockdown was underway, his marriage was ending, and a scheduled Milan appearance cancellation garnered an invitation to record at the Fazioli Pianoforti Concert Hall, annex to the renowned Italian piano manufactory in Sacile, Pordenone, about an hour northeast of Venice. At Fazioli, Sosa found himself in august company. Herbie Hancock and a host of classical pianists are Fazioli artists. Among the institutions that have embraced the Fazioli sound are the Juilliard School, Teatro La Fenice (Venice), the Budapest Palace of Arts, the Paris Conservatory, the Beijing Grand Theatre, and the universities of Salzburg, Graz, and Vienna. An unscripted two-hour solo improvisation on a Fazioli grand in the empty concert hall provided the raw audio for Sendas , later to be flavored in the mix, sparsely, with voice clips, percussion, loops, field recordings, found sounds effects that Sosa has collected over a career spanning four decades. As Sosa related to me soon after completing the post-production of Sendas , �Humanity is spiritually lost. We humans are all in this together. We need to evolve, but always keeping the traditions, walking with a strong, determined pace. We need more grounded music with overtones that resonate with the lower chakras� like throat singing, a mantra of the universal music.� �Creativity is about combining all your influences in a new way. I don�t aspire to be jazz, Latin, timba, reggaeton, classical. I avoid styles, but I respect the forms.� �I try not to think about how listeners will receive it but I do try to address their expectations, and go with the music to some other new place. Many free spirits come to listen, to be a part of the journey we are on.� Sosa laughs, �My son says, �Your niche is really small.� But the people who come really are there to be part of what we are going to do.� �Economics, technology, the streaming ear wash, algorithms all want to put you into a defined category � and so do many music journalists! The industry�s mentality is that any investment in artists must be defined by market categories to be profitable.� �But I play to be free of that,� Sosa says. �I play without thinking. There are no wrong notes. I love the first take. That�s the take, the natural voice of your soul. �Less is more� is a mantra in my life and music.� Consider the opening of �Inside the Spirit,� easing in leisurely, reaching over the keyboard into the resonant heart of the instrument, plucking and stroking the strings, teasing out a fuller resonance � only later to be embellished in the studio mix with light percussion and the muted Spanish-language refrain of a pregonero or street vendor, as might be heard in the calles of Havana or any other Latin American barrio. Sendas by Omar Sosa Moving from the secular to the sacred, �Deities Serenade� is an Afro-Cuban invocation of the shape-shifting divine, yet with ample room for ecumenical recasting in accord with a listener�s own self-location. �Inside My Soul� and �Something from Home� are Sosa works that to my ear may be an intuitive response to the distant call of Chopin�s "Nocturnes," to which Sosa says he listened every night for two years as a conservatory student in Cuba. Sendas by Omar Sosa �Caribbean Movement� and �Shirma� speak to Sosa�s rootedness in the lyrical, rhythmic, and harmonic heritage of the plantation islands where African and European cultures tragically entwined. In the violent forging of the world�s first truly modern people, social, cultural, linguistic, and musical displacements proved more flexible and accommodating than many of those same people, who shaped a contentious convergence of traditions into a changing same that persists into the unfolding present, ever yet to come. With expressive transcendence such as this, seeking to reduce the spiritual essence and inspiration of Sosa�s music to words is rather a fool�s errand. Better rather to listen, to contemplate, to perceive the pathway, to wander the sonic sendas coursing to the next way station without prejudice or preconception. To that end, Scott Price, Sosa�s longtime manager and friend relates, �We are using Sendas as the springboard for our first experiments in AI-generated Omar Sosa music videos.� Absent the opportunity to see and hear Sosa perform live, the palpable ideal, these ancillary audiovisual experiments further the ineffability of his artistic quest, the unique nature of the listening experience and all that ensues.

items._cn_summary: 古巴钢琴家 Omar Sosa 在意大利 Fazioli 钢琴厅进行两小时无脚本独奏即兴，原始录音后混入稀疏的人声采样、打击乐、循环、录音与拾得声响。专辑诞生于疫情封锁与个人生活变迁交织的节点，Sosa 拒绝风格归类，强调避免流派标签、尊重形式本身。音乐呈现冥想式的探索状态：琴弦被直接拨弄以激发泛音共鸣，后期以轻柔打击乐与极简叠录延伸声场。专辑探讨精神失落与传统演进的关系，倡导低脉轮共振的接地音乐语言。整体创作方法强调首次即兴的直觉性，遵循'少即是多'的美学准则，将四十年积累的影响以全新方式重组。

items.body: Neubauten's uncompromising debut album ‘Kollaps’ is 45 years old. Jeremy Allen explores the bombed-out terrain of their West Berlin and wonders if, despite the penurious conditions, it was easier to make art then Feral musicians emerging from the rubble of bombed-out West Berlin (as composer György Ligeti described it, "a surrealist cage in which all those inside are free") and creating themselves out of their own blood and guts very much feels like a tale from another age. In a world of coffee shop startups, utilitarian computer software and ersatz bedroom electronica as aural wallpaper, building your own percussive instruments from scrap might seem primitive, complex, redundant even. But in 1981, when Einstürzende Neubauten made Kollaps, it was revolutionary. For the briefest... The post Concrète Dschungel: Einstürzende Neubauten’s Kollaps At 45 appeared first on The Quietus.
items._cn_summary: Einstürzende Neubauten 1981年的首张专辑《Kollaps》迎来45周年纪念。这支乐队诞生于战后西柏林的废墟之中，成员用废弃金属、钢管等工业废料自制打击乐器，将施工现场的声响转化为音乐语言。评论者将这种原始创作方式置于当时的语境中审视——在咖啡馆创业文化与精致卧室电子乐泛滥的当下，自制打击乐器似乎显得原始而多余，但在1981年这却是颠覆性的艺术实践。乐评将这些音乐人比作从瓦砾中重生的野兽，用自己的血肉构建艺术身份，与作曲家Ligeti所描绘的'超现实主义牢笼'形成互文。整篇文章聚焦于乐队诞生的时代背景与创作理念，对专辑具体声响设计的描述有限。
