items.body: Review by memowakeman — Review originally posted at www.therocktologist.comA third exquisite offering. The talented Italian quartet Aether is back with an incredibly solid, mature, refined, and creative album, one that fans of jazz fusion, progressive rock, and music that appeals to the senses will enjoy from beginning to end. Across 43 minutes and six tracks, the musicians treat us to a series of sonic landscapes that range from relaxing to frenetic, from atmospheric to deeply sensory, moving seamlessly between rock, post-rock, ambient, and classical music. It all begins with "Oort Cloud," whose opening seconds are atmospheric and otherworldly, creating a contemplative, dark mood. Little by little, new elements and sounds emerge, making you feel as though you are floating through space, caught somewhere between uncertainty and curiosity, until everything erupts at the 2:30 mark and a new rhythm takes over, retaining that dark sound that at times reminds me of early-70s King Crimson. As the minutes go by, the band introduces more colors, with the keyboards becoming a crucial element. Nevertheless, the atmospheres created by the bass, guitar, and drums come together to form a truly fascinating sonic experience. Next comes "Vogon," where the bass maintains a steady pulse while the guitar, keyboards, and drums appear here and there, gradually moving from uncertainty toward a sense of resolution as a distinctly jazzy melody begins to take shape. The very distinctive voice of the theatrical Claudio Milano emerges to recite a poem, creating one of the album's most unique moments. Shortly after his voice fades away, the music explodes, and jazz gives way to rock, with Andrea Ferrari's guitar charging forward like a whirlwind of emotions, compelling you to move and simply enjoy the music. The sonic landscapes shift in fascinating ways on "Cinq Teintes, Quatre Cadres." It begins by creating spacious, otherworldly soundscapes that, after two and a half minutes, take on an almost psychedelic essence, thanks first to the hypnotic bass of Andrea Grumelli, who guides the way as the guitar, synths, and drums deliver a daring and wonderful blend of space rock and jazz. This is one of my favorite tracks on the album. "La M�lancolie Du Petit Prince" features Andrea Serino's piano as the central element and guiding force of this literary-inspired passage. Beyond the blend of jazz and classical music brought to life by the piano, I love the fretless bass and its wonderfully fluid, graceful notes. I am also particularly fond of the deliciously sensory percussion Matteo Ravelli plays at the beginning, which he later contrasts with his electronic devices. Another majestic moment arrives with "Panta Rei." Its eight minutes unleash the quartet's imagination and creativity, showing us that after three studio albums, these musicians understand one another exceptionally well and flow together naturally, not only as accomplished instrumentalists but, more importantly, as a band. And although there are several darker, denser moments, I love the balance they achieve, as we suddenly find ourselves immersed in passages that feel bright and full of promise. At one point, they even reminded me of Focus. And yes, progressive rock is very much present here. Finally, the album reaches its brilliant conclusion with "Swerve." Over the course of its ten minutes, Aether delivers the climax of the entire work, a clear testament to the evolution of their sound and their boundless creativity. The band brings together a rich mix of genres and emotions, allowing listeners to immerse themselves in progressive passages, profound atmospheres, and enveloping, emotionally charged textures. The rhythm and intensity gradually build from the halfway point onward, creating a sonic spectrum that makes you want to move with the music, feel it, savor every moment, and truly make it your own. Congratulations to Aether on such a solid release. I absolutely loved it.

items._cn_summary: 意大利四人乐队Aether的第三张专辑在四十三分钟内构建了六个跨风格的音景段落。专辑从氛围化的开场逐渐过渡到复杂的节奏段落，融合摇滚、后摇滚、爵士融合与古典元素。低提琴与钢琴在多首曲目中担任引导角色，无品贝斯演奏出流畅而优雅的线条，鼓手在原声打击与电子设备之间自由切换。键盘与合成器不断改变音色层次，使整体声音从空间迷失氛围转向迷幻色彩。部分曲目由乐队主唱以剧场化的方式朗诵诗歌文本，成为听觉上的特殊标记。乐队在器乐演奏与编曲逻辑上展现出成熟的默契，能够自然地在安静段落与爆发段落之间流动。意大利独立厂牌的发行背景与融合古典文学意象的小王子章节等元素，赋予作品一定的文化深度。

items.body: Review by DimitrisTheHead — One of my favorite albums of 1969 hands down. So many styles of music one can find here. Blues, psychedelia, jazz, classical, rock. All of them combined to provide a sample of proto-prog in the late 60s British scene. Songs like "Isadora", "Waterways", "Bathers", "Moth" are majestic. Geoff Nicholson delivers some really beautiful and heart-warming vocal harmonies. But, Dave Arbus steals the show here. With his electric violin and his flute, he blesses our ears with some enchanting melodies. This album really could be close to perfect, if it weren't for those free jazz/improvisations on the songs "Centaur woman" & "In the stable of the Sphinx" which in my opinion kind of mess up a little bit the whole atmosphere of the album.Nevertheless, this is a really strong album, that the fans of the early prog rock era should check out.
items._genre: proto-prog / psychedelic rock / blues rock / jazz fusion / progressive rock
items._cn_summary: 这张1969年的专辑融合了布鲁斯、迷幻摇滚、爵士与古典等多种元素，被认为是英国早期前卫摇滚的雏形之作。Geoff Nicholson的人声和声温暖而优美，Dave Arbus的电提琴与长笛演奏则贡献了整张专辑最具记忆点的旋律段落，营造出多层次的编曲质感。评论者对'Isadora'、'Waterways'、'Bathers'和'Moth'等曲目给予高度评价，认为它们具有宏伟壮丽的气质。然而，专辑中'Centaur woman'与'In the stable of the Sphinx'两首作品中的自由爵士即兴段落被认为破坏了整体氛围的统一性，使专辑未能达到完美的境界。整体而言，这是一张展现了跨界融合野心的作品，对早期前卫摇滚爱好者具有一定的参考价值。

items.body: Band: Antropoceno | Album: No Ritmo da Terra | Genre: Post-rock | Bandcamp The newest release from this experimental Brazilian act is a harsh and uncompromising record. Taking cues from glitch, avant-garde metal, and native folk, and with lyrics in Portuguese, Tupi, and Yoruba, No Ritmo da Terra is a truly autochthonous Brazilian album. The sound is often maximal, bursting with shining synths, biting guitars and rattling percussion.  Score: 77/100 Band: Beware of Gods | Album: Upon Whom the Last Light Descends III: Behead the Oracle | Genre: Sludge metal, Post-metal | Bandcamp Beware of Gods’ latest album is full of groovy riffs and punishing walls of biting distortion. This band deftly uses texture and atmosphere to paint pictures, and there are a lot of creative and unorthodox choices in how passages and phrases are composed. The sci-fi story the album tells meshes well with the oppressive soundscapes, and this is an instance of things like sound effects and spoken dialogue adding to the effect of the record. Score: 75/100 Band: Haken | Album: in a fever dream | Genre: Progressive metal | Bandcamp This is the most I’ve enjoyed a Haken release since The Mountain. On Haken’s last few LPs, the band had leaned into a form of melodic djent, which, while dazzlingly technical, lacked anything all that memorable, at least to my ear. This new EP sees them take a step back from that and dip their toes back into more Dream Theater-style prog metal. This isn’t just the blatant DT worship of their first two records, though. The band has matured their sound and put their own unique stamp on things. They also include some great moody alt-rock and electronic flourishes, a la Porcupine Tree/Steven Wilson. Score: 85/100 Band: Kolm | Album: Yūgen | Genre: Progressive rock | Bandcamp I like Kolm’s 2018 debut, Umbra, but it is also some of the most blatant and unashamed Tool worship I’ve ever heard. Eight years later, this L.A.-based trio is back with their sophomore album, Yūgen. Yūgen is still obviously deeply indebted to Tool, but the band has diversified their sound a bit. Cynic jumps out as an obvious influence, and they’ve also developed their songwriting and arrangements to be more uniquely their own. My main complaint here is that this is a very long record. A number of riffs and ideas feel drawn out, and the band definitely could have tightened things up. Beyond that, there are a lot of great textures, and the bandmembers are clearly skilled musicians. There are some nice electronic interludes, too. Ignoring the bloat, there’s a lot of good music here. Score: 71/100 Band: Otobo | Album: Inside Machines | Genre: Progressive rock | Bandcamp Otobo is a trio from Albany, NY, that plays a crunchy, aggressive band of progressive rock heavily influenced by alt-rock. The songs are all manageable lengths with minimal bloat, but they still contain exciting, dynamic composition. Noise rock, post-punk, and math rock get their turns in the spotlight, too. Otobo does a great job at keeping textures varied, and there’s a skilled balance of complex artiness and enjoyable hooks. The album does lose a bit of steam near the end, but it’s still solid overall. Score: 74/100 Band: Panopticon | Album: Det Hjemsøkte Hjertet | Genre: Post-metal | Bandcamp Billed as a conclusion to a trilogy of records (the others being …And Again into the Light and Rime of Memory), Det Hjemsøkte Hjertet, is another powerful and affecting release in Pantopicon’s discography. The soundscapes swell and bristle, exploding with scouring-yet-abstract black metal riffs. Bluegrass and other forms of American folk music are prominent. Panopticon has a definite sound, so there’s only so much that can be said here that wouldn’t just be describing other records. But this features many of the band’s strongest elements. Score: 82/100

Tightly focused, rhythm-driven, and impactful Serge Geyzel‘s range of sonic motion knows no boundaries. So I Leave dives headfirst into bass-heavy frequencies and downtempo dub wobble, especially on the opening track, “So I Leave (feat. Ananoda),” a fiercely powerful blend of dark breaks and ultra-low-end pressure. “Don’t Like” pushes further into glitch ’n’ bass, braindance breakbeats, acid, and melodic tension, functioning like a signature centerpiece that could run infinitely. Closing with the dark breaks assault of “Sometimes Is a Sample (Serge Geyzel and Dagga),” the EP expands into experimental glitch, old-school funk, and surreal-infused mayhem, keeping this short run tightly focused, rhythm-driven, and impactful. items.album: [2View] Drift :: Manic EP / Radius Etc :: Alive & Thriving EP (The Consumers Research and Development Label)
items.excerpt: The Consumers Research and Development Label is clearly not trying to be one thing, and that’s the most encouraging part of this reintroduction. A techno veteran finally putting out his own record after twenty years of platforming everyone else, sitting right next to a hip-hop travelogue built out of literal years of instability and constant movement, that’s a genuinely odd pairing on paper, and it works precisely because neither release is compromising to fit next to the other. &nbs
items.body: The Consumers Research and Development Label is clearly not trying to be one thing, and that’s the most encouraging part of this reintroduction. A techno veteran finally putting out his own record after twenty years of platforming everyone else, sitting right next to a hip-hop travelogue built out of literal years of instability and constant movement, that’s a genuinely odd pairing on paper, and it works precisely because neither release is compromising to fit next to the other.   Consumers finds its second wind Manic by Drift   Alive & Thriving by Radius Etc   There’s a good story behind why this review exists at all. The Consumers Research and Development Label ran independently through the 2000s before becoming an imprint of Someoddpilot Records, the Chicago label-turned-agency that also handled branding for Pitchfork back when that meant something specific in the industry, and later built brand identity work for clients like Drag City, Jagjaguwar, and Secretly Canadian. Geoffrey Wilson bought Consumers in 2023 with help from Chris Eichenseer, who founded Someoddpilot in 1999 and who Wilson had shared an office with from 2003 to 2008, before the label originally shut down. Somewhere in the years between closing and reopening, a flood destroyed the entire back stock. Whatever’s floating around on Discogs or eBay now is all that survived physically; the rest is gone. The label came back properly in November 2024 with a showcase at Public Works in Wicker Park, quiet after that, and this is its real reintroduction to a wider audience: two EPs, two very different sounds, one label figuring out what it wants to be the second time around. Drift’s Manic comes first and it’s a strange kind of debut for someone who’s clearly not new to any of this. Sean Krainik has run Parotic Records, the Midwest techno label, for over two decades, putting out records from DJ Slip, Johannes Heil, Matt Paffel, Dave Olson, and Mr. Projectile among others. He never released his own music on vinyl until now. Manic pulls from more than twenty years of writing tracks in the background while other people’s records took priority, and that accumulated time shows in how confidently unshowy this record is. This leans techno and IDM more than anything experimental, dancefloor-facing and beat-heavy across the whole tracklist. The title track builds itself up layer by layer into a pulsating beat while TV dialogue keeps pulling focus sideways, a small disruption that never fully resolves. Nothing here is trying to be difficult, and nothing here needed to be. “R$W” and “Osmosis” are the two that stick hardest. Different rhythms, same underlying intent—Krainik chasing something gritty and repetitive at once, loops that don’t evolve so much as they insist on themselves. Baby Ford‘s influence is audible in how minimal and slightly off-center the drum programming stays, that same stripped tension where less becomes the entire point rather than a limitation working against the track. “Murderer’s Row” leans into that same lineage even more directly, carrying an unintended tribute to Throbbing Gristle in its haze and darkness, deliberately murky where the rest of the EP stays brighter. It’s dance music built by someone who spent twenty years listening to other people make dance music, which sounds like it should produce something derivative and instead produces something oddly assured. He knows exactly which two or three elements a track actually needs and refuses to add a fourth just because he can.   Two EPs, two very different sounds :: Radius Etc‘s Alive & Thriving sits nowhere near that world. This is instrumental hip-hop pushed somewhere stranger, call it hip-hop IDM for lack of a cleaner label, though the term undersells how much dub techno and straight experimental electronic music bleeds into the beats underneath. Norwood recorded this across a blur of hostels, planes, and temporary housing between 2021 and 2025, and the press notes frame it explicitly as documentation of moving from housing instability and food scarcity into something closer to self-actualization. A travel document, in his own words, proof of surviving into thriving. That context sits underneath the music without ever being spelled out inside the tracks themselves, which is the right call. The record doesn’t lecture you about where it came from. It just carries the weight of it. “Goldenlocks” is the standout, and it’s also the most straightforwardly hip-hop beat on the record, except the tempo keeps breaking and the snares reverse and catch themselves mid-hit like the whole beat is tripping over its own feet on purpose. There’s a video for it, one of three the label produced for this release. Little vocal samples surface throughout, adding texture without ever becoming a hook. “Stuttering Spaces (PoplockJam)” goes fully electro, upbeat in a way nothing else on the record quite matches, the most purely fun three minutes here. “One 4 Larry Heard Pt. 1” is the only track running a straight 4/4 kick and it’s catchy specifically because it doesn’t try to be clever about it, same DNA as everything surrounding it just aimed squarely at a dancefloor instead of a headspace. The “Pt. 1” leaves you wondering if there’s a Pt. 2 coming or if the numbering is its own quiet joke about unfinished business. “Go Inside/Outside” is the most abstract piece on the record, a loop cycling endlessly through filters and phasers and pitch shifts like a revolving door that never fully closes, always mid-swing. The Consumers Research and Development Label is clearly not trying to be one thing, and that’s the most encouraging part of this reintroduction. A techno veteran finally putting out his own record after twenty years of platforming everyone else, sitting right next to a hip-hop travelogue built out of literal years of instability and constant movement, that’s a genuinely odd pairing on paper, and it works precisely because neither release is compromising to fit next to the other. They just happen to share a home. If these two EPs are the tone-setters for what Consumers wants to be in its second life, the label picked back up somewhere considerably more interesting than where it left off two decades ago. Drift‘s Manic and Radius Etc‘s Alive & Thriving are both available on The Consumers Research and Development Label. Manic by Drift    The post [2View] Drift :: Manic EP / Radius Etc :: Alive & Thriving EP (The Consumers Research and Development Label) first appeared on Igloo Magazine.

items.body: Landscape 07 unfolds in breaths: slow waves advance, overlap, recede and return in subtly altered forms. The movement is continuous, yet it can escape a distracted listener. You need to stop, allow the piece to find its own pace and follow its changes as you might follow shadows moving across a field. An accomplished expression of stillness, physical presence and transformation landscape 07 by fields we found / quiet details   Fields We Found is the alias of British musician, mastering engineer and visual artist Alex Gold, who founded the quiet details label in 2023. Following releases on Home Normal, Seil Records, handstitched*, and Ambientologist, Gold has increasingly focused his work on extended listening. The Landscape series grew out of compositions created for his personal meditation practice; over time, the creative process itself also became a form of meditation. Landscape 07, the seventh installment in the series, runs for more than twenty-five minutes. It is an extended live performance constructed from electronic instruments, tape and successive layers of sound. The piece begins almost without a threshold. A broad sound emerges from the haze, already inhabited by tremors, gentle fluctuations and distant trails. During the opening minutes, the music gains weight; the volume rises calmly and glimmers of light move across its surface. From here, Landscape 07 unfolds in breaths: slow waves advance, overlap, recede and return in subtly altered forms. The movement is continuous, yet it can escape a distracted listener. You need to stop, allow the piece to find its own pace and follow its changes as you might follow shadows moving across a field. “Later, individual lines drift apart and the landscape opens out. This is where the title finds its true meaning. The horizon remains; the light changes. It is a slow transformation, free of spectacular gestures, shaped by passages that can be felt before they can be defined.” ~Mirco Salvadori The presence of tape can be felt in the sound’s internal movement. The notes have porous edges, slight instabilities and a warmth far removed from artificial stillness. Even when everything appears motionless, something continues to shift. The overall balance gradually changes, brighter colours surface and the mass of sound seems to lift. Later, individual lines drift apart and the landscape opens out. This is where the title finds its true meaning. The horizon remains; the light changes. It is a slow transformation, free of spectacular gestures, shaped by passages that can be felt before they can be defined. Gold handles duration with patience and restraint. Each event is allowed to remain long enough to alter our perception of everything around it. In its central section, the piece takes on a darker, more introspective colour. Threads and reflections continue to move through the texture; through headphones, they reveal small lateral movements, like currents. Light then returns gradually and the music expands without losing its composure. This leads to the point of greatest emotional intensity, reached through patient accumulation. The journey feels natural, almost as though it had formed by itself, while retaining the freedom of a gesture made in the moment. The piece asks for a simple kind of openness: to remain, to listen, to give each nuance time to reveal itself and to accept that the inner landscape may change alongside the sonic one. In these passages, distant echoes of German electronic music from the early 1970s begin to surface. The more abstract expanses of Tangerine Dream’s Zeit, the cosmic materiality of early Klaus Schulze and some of Cluster’s suspended atmospheres come to mind in the way timbre becomes form. Fields We Found keeps everything on an intimate, tactile scale. The connection lies in the trust placed in machines, in their natural drift and in the time a sound needs to reveal its hidden folds. Recording the performance directly to tape preserves the element of risk that gives life to such a gradual process. “A single sound remains, along with tape hiss and a few distant reflections; eventually, these elements also slip beneath the threshold of perception.” ~Mirco Salvadori An even closer affinity leads to Éliane Radigue. Landscape 07 shares the French composer’s attentiveness to what can emerge from within a prolonged sound and to the variations that appear when the ear stops searching for a melody. The historical and poetic distance remains clear; the surface here is denser and more explicitly ambient. Yet the kind of listening it requires is close to Radigue’s: focused, patient and ready to recognise an event within apparent stillness. Pauline Oliveros’ Deep Listening also comes to mind, particularly in its understanding of attention as an active part of the work, as does Suzanne Ciani, in the gentle way electronic sound can suggest physical movement. Towards the end, the piece begins to subtract. The pressure recedes, its lines grow sparse and what remains reveals its irregularities more clearly. The farewell becomes fragile. The long fade avoids any emphatic sense of closure. A single sound remains, along with tape hiss and a few distant reflections; eventually, these elements also slip beneath the threshold of perception. It is an ending fully consistent with the work as a whole: the ear is left to measure the disappearance, while the silence that follows seems to last a little longer. Landscape 07 succeeds because its calmness contains tension. Meditation here has density, pressure and material memory. The instruments breathe, the tapes impart instability and depth, and the studio work preserves the spontaneity of the performance. With each new listen, the hierarchy of details changes: something that first seemed marginal becomes a guide, a fluctuation turns into rhythm, a blur acquires definition. This is music that entrusts its richness to time and draws its strength from time in return. A remarkable entry in the series, and perhaps its most accomplished expression of stillness, physical presence and transformation. Landscape 07 is available on quiet details. items.body: Jesu Aparicio is a Spanish artist who sees himself first and foremost as a DJ, and only secondly as a producer. He has been active in the Spanish club scene for years and won me over this year with his album “Human Control”. The album was released on Jesu’s own label, Espacio Cielo, in collaboration with Mots Music. The name Parissior may not ring a bell for many, but I highly recommend this work to anyone with an interest in Dark-Techno and EBM. The album’s title and theme reflect the increasingly complex relationship between humans, technology, control, and the systems that shape our daily lives. By combining dark electronic sounds with an atmosphere that is both unsettling and intriguing, Parissior creates music that invites the listener to look beyond the surface. The album evokes the atmosphere and danceability of the 1990s Frankfurt Techno scene while adding a distinctly contemporary twist. For me, this record is one of this year’s best discoveries, making it the perfect time to meet the artist behind Parissior and talk to him about “Human Control”, his influences, and his approach to music. (Courtesy by Inferno Sound Diaries) Parissior interview Q: Could you give us some background on your musical activities, which apparently began quite some time ago as a DJ and eventually evolved into producing, leading to the Parissior project? Jesu: I began DJing professionally in my native Cantabria in 2001, playing Techno and House under my own name, ‘Jesu Aparicio’. In 2004, I moved to Salamanca, where I became a resident DJ at several venues, including Cubic Club, Submarino and Beatz. Those years were a major learning experience for me and gave me a much deeper understanding of the music industry. I eventually opened my own venue, Clavel Ocho, which featured an upstairs floor dedicated to Electronic music called Espacio Cielo – the name I would later revive for my record label. I started producing around 2004 and, over the years, explored many different styles and released music under several aliases. Altogether, I have released more than 600 tracks. I have always considered myself a DJ first and a producer second, although these days I actually spend more time producing music than performing as a DJ. Around 2011, I began to feel restricted by playing the same styles, so I created the Parissior alias as a way to broaden my musical horizons. It allowed me to explore funkier and more cosmic sounds, as well as Electro and Italo-Disco, eventually moving towards the EBM-influenced sound that has become an important part of the project’s identity. Q: Personally, I find it interesting that you moved into music production after starting out as a DJ – a role that naturally exposes you to a vast amount of music. This perhaps also helps explain the eclectic nature of your own work. What did your experience as a DJ bring to your approach to music-making, and what were some of your key influences and muses? Jesu: As a DJ, I have always been very eclectic and curious, and I have always enjoyed collecting music from a wide range of genres: ’80s music, Funk and Soul, Disco, Electro, House, Techno, Big Beat, Breaks… Salamanca had many clubs and bars, each with a very distinct musical identity, so playing there pushed you to dig deeper, discover new sounds and adapt to very different audiences. Being exposed to such a vast amount of music has undoubtedly had a major influence on the way I produce. You learn to recognize the formulas and ideas that make each genre work, and then reinterpret and adapt them to your own musical language. My influences have naturally evolved over the years, but I could never leave out Joy Division and New Order, Talking Heads, The Prodigy, The Chemical Brothers, Pet Shop Boys, Andrew Weatherall, Primal Scream or LCD Soundsystem, among many others. Q: You released the album “Human Control” this year, which, as I understand it, was not originally conceived as an album. How did it all come about, and how did the concept of “Human Control” take shape? Or did the concept emerge only afterwards, almost imposing itself on the music? Jesu: As you rightly say, the album was not initially planned as such. I had three tracks that I had deliberately held back from releasing on any label because they felt more personal, less focused on the dancefloor, and did not really fit with any of the EPs I had previously released. Almost without realizing it, I had incorporated phrases and messages into those tracks that shared a certain underlying theme: a defense of the analogue world and a critique of the artificiality and falsehood that often surround today’s digital culture and social media. Once I recognized that common thread, I decided to compose a series of new tracks around those original three and gradually shape the whole thing into an album. The first track I created with that intention was “Human Control.” It features a sample from a speech by Greta Thunberg at the UN Climate Action Summit, in which she delivers a passionate and somewhat dramatic rebuke to the world’s leaders. That track ultimately gave both the album and its central concept a clear identity. Q: What can you tell us about the writing and production process behind the album? What did you focus on most, and what were the different stages you went through to bring “Human Control” to completion? What tools and equipment did you work with, and what were the biggest challenges along the way? Jesu: One of the album’s defining features – and also its biggest challenge – was the decision to deliberately limit the amount of hardware and software I used on each track. I find that working within those kinds of restrictions forces me to be more creative, especially compared with having thousands of possibilities available in the form of plug-ins. My process was generally to choose a small palette of sound sources for each track, record the main parts, and then reshape and develop them through processing. For example, every synthesizer part on “True Connection” came from the Waldorf Pulse 2. Most of the basslines on the album were created with an analogue clone of the Roland SH-101, which I also used to design many of the drum sounds, while the Acid lines came from the Behringer TD-3. Another synthesizer that played a major role throughout the album was the Model D, and I also incorporated parts I had recorded years earlier with my Roland JX-3P. On the software side, I used Ableton’s stock plug-ins alongside Massive and Omnisphere. Massive was the only synthesizer used on “Human Control,” while Omnisphere appears more sparingly on some of the other tracks, mainly providing polyphonic textures. I also enjoy running synthesizers through effects pedals to create new tones and textures, while the vocals were processed using the Roland VT-4 and a variety of VST effects. Ultimately, the main focus was to get as much character and variety as possible from a relatively small and carefully chosen set of tools. Q: With this album, you explore themes such as digital identity, technology, artificial validation, and the relationship between humans and machines. Could you tell us a little more about these themes, and to what extent did they influence your decision to release the album on vinyl? To me, the physical format almost feels like a response to – or a reaction against – the increasingly digital nature of our lives. And if so, why vinyl rather than cassette? Jesu: That was exactly the idea. Releasing the album on vinyl was, in many ways, a reaction against the digitalisation of almost every aspect of our lives. Particularly since the pandemic, it often feels as though people’s lives have been reduced to the online alter egos they create on platforms such as Instagram – showing the world only what they want others to see and projecting lifestyles that they are not necessarily living in reality. Releasing a record on vinyl had also been unfinished business for me with Espacio Cielo, so my own album felt like the perfect opportunity to take that step. There was an economic reason as well: digital sales are falling every year as listening increasingly shifts towards streaming platforms such as Spotify, yet the royalties these services pay are extremely unfair. Sometimes you barely earn enough to buy a hamburger, which makes it very difficult for an independent label to remain financially sustainable. I also feel that digital music is more ephemeral. It disappears more quickly, becomes outdated faster and struggles to hold people’s attention. A vinyl record has a physical presence and a sense of permanence: people tend to spend more time with it, and it can remain part of their lives for years. In that sense, the format became a natural extension of the album’s concept. To be honest, I never seriously considered releasing it on cassette. It is a very nostalgic format, but I also think that very few people still own the equipment needed to play tapes. Of course, the same issue exists to some extent with vinyl, but many DJs have kept their Technics turntables, and the fact that the company has released new models such as the MK7 gives me some reason for optimism. Vinyl also has a much stronger connection to my own history as a DJ and to the culture surrounding this music. From now on, we plan to slow down the label’s digital release schedule and gradually release more records on vinyl. Who knows – perhaps in a few years we will release exclusively on vinyl. It is something I am seriously considering. Q: Where do you draw the line today between human control and the control we voluntarily surrender to technology? In what sense do you see the title and concept of “Human Control” as a warning, an observation, or perhaps even a personal confession? How do you see humans evolving alongside technological progress, and what role do you think the musician will play in that relationship? Jesu: That boundary is becoming increasingly blurred. There is no denying that we will benefit enormously from technological progress and that it will make many aspects of our lives easier. However, when it comes to art and culture, I believe we need to preserve certain principles and ensure that convenience and automation do not replace human intention, creativity and genuine expression. In that sense, “Human Control” is both an observation and a warning. Technology itself is not the enemy; the real question is how much control and creative autonomy we are willing to surrender to it. We should remain the ones making the decisions, with technology serving as a tool rather than dictating the creative process. At the same time, I think a counter-movement is beginning to emerge – one that will bring back a greater appreciation for craftsmanship, physical formats and live music. I am already seeing clubs programming exclusively live sets, as well as all-vinyl nights, which I find very encouraging. Perhaps the musician’s role in this new relationship will be precisely to preserve that human element: spontaneity, imperfection and a genuine connection with the audience. Q: Do you also perform your Parissior tracks live, or do they mainly form part of your DJ sets? How does that work in practice, and what can we expect from Parissior in the near future? Jesu: I have always considered myself more of a DJ than a producer, even though, since the pandemic, I have actually spent more time producing than performing. I love playing DJ sets, and while I already have enough of my own material prepared to develop a full live show, the right opportunity has not yet presented itself. For the moment, Parissior’s music therefore appears mainly within my DJ sets. I have performed hybrid sets using hardware, but fees are sometimes so limited today that paying for additional luggage to transport equipment becomes impractical. The same applies to vinyl: I play vinyl locally, but when I travel, I usually perform with CDJs for exactly the same reason. Because of my day job, I only play around five or six gigs a year, and promoters generally approach me to perform DJ sets. However, I would definitely like to explore the live format when the right opportunity and conditions come along. About Parissior Parissior is the alias of Spanish DJ and producer Jesu Aparicio. He began DJing professionally in his native Cantabria in 2001 under his own name, playing Techno and House. In 2004 he moved to Salamanca, where he became a resident DJ at venues including Cubic Club, Submarino and Beatz, and later opened his own venue, Clavel Ocho, whose upstairs floor, Espacio Cielo, was dedicated to electronic music. He started producing around 2004 and has released more than 600 tracks under various aliases. He created the Parissior alias in 2011 to explore Electro, Italo-Disco and EBM-influenced sounds beyond his earlier productions. Parissior has released singles and EPs since at least 2016, including “Could I Drown In Your Desire” and “Dance To The Groove” (Spa In Disco), followed by “Let Them Dance” (Hot Digits Music, 2017) and further EPs and compilation appearances for Golden Soul Records. From “Back To Earth” (2020) onward he has worked mainly through Espacio Cielo, the label he revived from his former venue’s name, releasing further singles, EPs and compilation tracks including “Battle Cry” (2021), “Raver In The Booth” and “Full of Stars” (2023), and the Skylax release “Antennae” (2024). “Human Control”, Parissior’s first full-length album, was released on Espacio Cielo in collaboration with Mots Music. Side-Line reviewed the album in September 2026, describing it as a mix of Dark-Techno and EBM. This interview follows that review.

items.body: To celebrate and commemorate John Coltrane’s 100 th birthday, drummer extraordinaire Don Berman will reprise at the Chapel Performance Space in Seattle his original composition, 'Ascension Northwest', written in the spirit of Coltrane’s Ascension (Impulse!, 1966). As in the original, Berman has11 musicians playing a series of mantras interspersed with spirited soloing over improvised support from subsets of other players, including a double-bass duet. A preview of this year’s performance written by Paul Rauch appears in Seattle’s Earshot Jazz magazine: https://online.fliphtml5.com/risyt/Earshot_Jazz_09_2026/#p=13 You can hear earlier versions of 'Ascension Northwest' released here: https://threshold24.bandcamp.com/album/ascension‑northwest As a contribution for the FJB Coltrane birthday column, I’ve asked the 11 musicians performing 'Ascension Northwest' (myself included) to reflect on Coltrane’s Ascension and its impact on their musical journey. Below, our answers (gingerly edited). The questionnaire is reproduced at the very end. Tom Varner (French horn) 1. I knew about Coltrane and loved his music from his time with Miles, and also his ‘classic’ quartet recordings, when I was in high school and getting into jazz. I did not know about Ascension until a bit later, perhaps early in college. Even though I loved Ornette Coleman, and even Albert Ayler, I must say that very late Coltrane and Ascension was a bit :”Whoa! This is too heavy for me!” at first listen. I think I wanted to hear the ‘melodic line’ no matter how ‘out’ it was, and this music went beyond that. Eventually I grew to love it, letting go of the ‘I must hear a clear line’ worry and just enjoying being carried away in the power of the SOUND. I.e., that sound of a ‘scary but then NOT scary’ glorious totality of several improvisers all going full steam ahead at once. The JCOA Michael Mantler ‘Communications’ 3-LP set, from 1968, with Pharoah Sanders and other greats, was a kind of bridge for me to the world of Ascension . To a kind of ‘beautiful crying battle’ as opposed to just noise. Within one or two years, I was open to playing in those settings! 1a. Ascension opened up a new world of “multiple new sound-creating improvisers” creating new avenues that were not ‘just’ chord change or single-line orientated. From then on, Coltrane’s world and the worlds of, say, Xenakis and Ligeti, were not so far apart! 1b.Moving into the ‘90s, I worked with ensembles that had 6, 7, 8 winds with bass and drums. I was going for that high energy sound where it was ‘ok’ to not hear individual single lines and just get swept away in the sound. The best example of this is my own “Death at the Right Time,” on “The Mystery of Compassion” on Soul Note (1992). 5 saxes, three low brass, bass and drums. 1c. Ascension kind of gave us ‘permission’ to create beautiful and powerful structures with very little or no written music, just ideas, and trusting that the improvisers will create a lasting artwork on the spot. I love that! 2. This is very corny, but at age 18, I clearly remember thinking “Well, remember, Tom, if things get bad in the future, or very challenging, don’t forget to listen to Coltrane—that music is healing. That music will always be there.” And, I would also simply say, “thank you, Mr. Coltrane.” Jim Knodle (trumpet) I heard Ascension when it was released in 1966. I regard it as a companion to Ornette's double quartet project Free Jazz . The interaction between Scott LaFaro and Jimmy Garrison is really something! Perry Robinson told me that the whole thing started at the Federal Prison in Lexington where everyone practiced in the same room at the same time. They didn’t want them to rehearse, so they just played ad hoc . Kenny Mandell (alto sax) 1. I was probably 19 when I first heard Ascension . 1972 or so. Being in college, I had heard free jazz players in NYC, and I knew Sun Ra’s music. Ascension was way more organized than a lot of Sun Ra’s music insofar as it kept the traditional jazz form where there was thematic material followed by solos. There are motifs but there aren’t any chord changes to speak of, and there is some degree of cacophony. Depending on the player, some of the solos were more traditional, others were, I would say, divinely inspired, like Eric Dolphy’s. In my listening life at that time, I quickly went from Led Zeppelin to the Art Ensemble, Albert Ayler, Archie Shepp, and Cecil Taylor. Most people thought I was crazy. I related to the energy of it. The dissonance never bothered me per se. Ascension showed me that the big band format could be stretched. The rock stuff was relatively static in comparison. Hendrix was close. Everybody else stayed in the form. I see Ascension as important but not seminal. It’s certainly part of the canon. 1b. I’ve put many large groups together over the years. Part of the game plan for large group improvisation is to establish a level of trust. I’ve learned to pick people who are comfortable recognizing that the traditional limits or strictures put on playing are actually optional, and one can use or not use those depending on what sort of statement the whole piece wants to make. Murray Bookchin’s Post-Scarcity Anarchism (1971, 1986) was pivotal (early 1970s) for me as much as any of this music. I tried to use those principles in music and in organizing. My book some day will be called The Tyranny of Harmony . Piano chords in particular limit your choices as an improvisor. It’s also the case that as I’ve gotten older and found that the audience just hasn’t been there for totally unstructured, large-form music, I’ve tended to select pieces or write pieces that give the audience some sort of repeated motif to ground their listening experience. 1c. Ascension opened the door. After A Love Supreme (1965), people thought Coltrane took an extreme left turn into the world of sound exploration as it could be manifested in improvisation and group interaction. Ascension put into stark reality the challenges of making and of listening to that kind of music. I don’t think they got to the level that the Art Ensemble of Chicago did over the years, and some of Cecil’s groups that stayed together for years: Jimmy Lyons, Sirone, Andrew Cyrille, they practiced incessantly and got telepathic. 2. John Coltrane had an obsession with achieving a certain sound. Coltrane—his essence for me–is that ceaseless searching. This is what I love about music probably the most, it’s that it never ends. Dick Valentine (tenor sax) I reflected at length on the questions you posed, and on the evolution of my attitudes, responses and relations with Coltrane’s music, which I understand in a context of almost 60 years trying to educate myself and participate in contemporary expressions of Great Black Music. In the end, despite that his recorded output made a tremendous impact on my playing ‑‑ and was a singular factor in motivating my drive to make music ‑‑ I think it fair to say Ascension , the recording, has not occupied as big a space in my development or conceptualization as some other works. I played in Don Berman's three presentations of Ascension Northwest in 2016, and I'm very pleased indeed to get to do it again on the Coltrane centenary. I really cherish the privilege of participating with artists the caliber of those whom Don has persuaded. I look around the room at the assemblage of musical knowledge, emotional depth, technical proficiency, and aesthetic ambition, I am inspired and amazed and humbled. I’m long past accepting that I will never "understand" society. It seems to me the “order that governs power and human relations” in our real world is founded on out‑of‑date assumptions regarding what humanity needs to flourish. I know that there are many people aware of this damaging misalignment, and I can tell they mostly share my frustration that fixing large‑scale misalignments is not in the offing, thanks precisely to the systems that govern the distribution of power and dictate humans' relationship with real resources. So, on John Coltrane's centenary, we'll gather musicians, players and audience in celebration. In a sense, a roomful is perhaps a model of “society.” Everyone in the room will have some mental image of what constitutes a successful event ‑‑ in context, the definition of the community “flourishing,” right? As players, we have the responsibility to provide physical, audible inputs to the outcome. There is a bit of magic to what may happen here. Each player contributes to the global fabric, whose nature he may not predict. It’s understood that coordinated inputs are in some sense a prerequisite for success, and communication is required for coordination. How is communication achieved? By the act that constitutes that player’s input. It’s a bit recursive, to say the least! Neil Welch (tenor sax) 1. Ascension came my way when I was 15 or 16. I picked up the album in cd format at a record store. This was my first experience with Trane’s music on Impulse!. I picked up the album out of curiosity. I was initially struck by three things: 1. The album cover ‑‑ Coltrane the seeker, looking beyond himself, and beyond us to something cosmic. 2. The length of the album: Until this point, I didn't know that a ‘jazz’ album could be +/‑ 40 minutes in length. 3. The cd version had takes 1 and 2, which made it a double album. It was the most expensive CD I had ever bought. The response for me was immediate. I felt the album opened with a declarative question. Coltrane begins with a theme, but it is incomplete. The tonic is ‘missing’ from the first note he plays. He asks the band a question with only the partial theme, and leaves it to the band to complete that theme. Ascension felt to me a major and inevitable document in Coltrane’s music from this period. The emotional intensity of his solos, and what he was asking of a small group, had reached a tipping point. I found it deeply humbling and revealing that he used the vehicle of a communal sound to further amplify the concept of the jazz musician as soloist and group collaborator. 1a. After Ascension , I understood that in musical conversation, a powerful theme could be stated with brevity. A short theme can grant space for a complex response of virtually any length. 1b. Ascension helped me to experience song length as a durational mind-set. A song could, and ought to be, exactly the length needed to fulfill its musical and emotional aims. 1c .Ascension is, for me, an album of colliding forces and the unity of embracing those forces towards a common mission. It’s like people in a building. All these souls one floor atop the other. Different lives, worldviews, needs, hurts, wants, but all share the same vertical massing. If that building is on fire, they are invested in each other's outcome. They’ve looked in the eyes of those people in the elevator. 2. Can we as a society still sit with, and grapple with in real time, discordance in art‑making? Can intensity of sound and emotion hold space for us in our lives and aid us in the journey of deeper personal growth? Steve Meyer (alto sax) 1. I must have been 14 or 15. I was just getting into Coltrane and came across Ascension at my local record store. At that point I’d only known some of his earlier quartet work and work with Miles. Seeing that this was a larger group piqued my interest. And I recognized the names of a lot of heavy players, though I doubt I’d heard most of them at that point, so thought it would be a good album. After getting back home, I’m in my bedroom and put on the album. I don’t know what I was expecting but not too far into the first side (the first ensemble part) I knew it wasn’t for me. I didn’t know what to make of it, and it didn’t speak to me. I think I finished the first side but didn’t listen to the second. A few years went by before I was ready to give it another try. I was still an adventurous listener, so my first reaction didn’t turn me off from listening to other “out”/free musics which I grew to appreciate and enjoy more and more. 1a. If I don’t like what I hear on first listen, I remind myself that there are works of art out there that I’m not ready for. Music will speak to us when we’re ready to hear it. 1b. While I was listening to more out music in my teens it was years later before I played free music – at least with others. In high school this wasn’t the kind of music most of my musician friends would be into. Even with the one or two who weren’t opposed to it, we never thought to attempt it ourselves, at least not in any serious way, sticking to more standard jazz and the fusion music of the day. (This is early 80s, btw.) Even later, people I played with tended to be more conventional in the foundation of their music. These days I’m fortunate to have a community of musicians who embrace free/creative music. And, I have more confidence in myself to nudge the conversation that way when playing with others that I think will be receptive to it. 1c. I tend to not view music through a sociological lens, but Ascension and similar music has made me consider the normative orders of music in the US. Mainly, they’ve shown me there are a lot of stories to be told and a lot of different ways to tell them. 2. I want to thank Coltrane for his music and inspiration. The question to ask myself: how can I harness the focus and questing spirit of Trane? Eric Ring (piano) While A Love Supreme was life changing at 18, I’d surprisingly never heard Ascension prior to preparing for this performance. Don Berman (composer, drums ) 1. A sax player at my summer Maine resort job, a student of Jackie McLean, had introduced me to Coltrane’s Live at Birdland (Impulse!, 1964). This was 1972. I heard an amazing spiritual element in John Coltrane's music when I heard his quartet play “Alabama.” It struck me incredibly deeply and I have adored jazz and playing jazz ever since. (The piece was a deeply moving eulogy to the victims of bombing of the 16th street Baptist church in Birmingham, Alabama.) A couple of years later, in my junior year of college, I heard Ascension and realized that Trane had helped jazz expand its scope enormously to express a wider range of feelings. With the Ascension session, jazz composition and form had evolved light years from the beginnings of jazz decades earlier. After Ascension , there was now a huge universe of possibilities for jazz musicians to explore in their work. 1a.As I got further into jazz I particularly loved Miles Davis and John Coltrane, because I saw how each had evolved continuously throughout their musical journeys, from one period and chapter and style to another. The way I think about music and music making after Ascension is part and parcel of how I feel about music and art in general. All of the art forms have a rich and magical history. If you have studied and played music for years and years, you have to discover who you are and what your aesthetic is. 1b. For me, Ascension is part of what guided me further into freer playing and improvising in the last 20 years. Creating my own compositions has become more important for me. I organize pieces that contain both written and improvised sections. For this I select musicians that can both interpret written compositions and also improvise very well. 2. I would ask others: How does Coltrane’s music move you and make you feel about what feelings or sounds you play and express when you play? The world is full of a truly amazing variety of music. There are masters playing in each of those styles. I would ask others who take music seriously to open their minds and make sure they hear the music of master creators, live when possible, and in as many styles as possible. Master the basic fundamentals, and take music as seriously as Trane did. For those just seeking fun, that is fine too. A lot of striving people in the arts take things too seriously, especially when they become too self-absorbed and their egos interfere with what they are attempting to do as musicians. As the great pianist and educator Kenny Werner teaches his students and readers, “your value as a human being is not based upon how well you play a musical instrument.” Gregg Miller (baritone sax) 1. Around 1997 I bought a used CD copy of the compilation, The Major Works of John Coltrane (GRP Records, 1992) which included both takes of Ascension as well as Om , Kulu Se Mama , and Selflessness . I was stunned at the difference in intent between those recordings and Giant Steps . In Giant Steps , I heard a restless cramming of as many notes as quickly as possible within structures that could barely contain them. In Ascension , Coltrane had left that set of problems behind in favor of a compositional form that foregrounded the free-playing (and listening, or not listening) of every other player, a dense maelstrom that produced its own power without regard to or in opposition to or transcending of the traditional tropes of organized sound. To my ears, there was still an evident structuredness to the resultant noise, but full-on interplay was now the method and the lesson. It felt to me like a releasing of mutual respect, a lifting of repression inherent in most musics, and a deliberate shifting of power dynamics from a singular ordered mind that commands obedience (and players willingly, often reverently submitting to that control) to the shared embrace of others who jointly participate. Messy, but beautiful. I was studying a lot of Habermas at the time, and so for me, the link between music-making and communicative action was an easy one to see/hear and understand. I wasn’t playing free music (or any music) at the time, but the seed had been sown without me knowing it. 1a. In the late 1990s I would listen to Ascension and the other tracks on Major Works over and again while studying. It was the kind of music that permitted my mind to roam freely and/or easily concentrate elsewhere without demanding I enter its rhythms, melodies, cadence. There was something liberating in its power to shape time and experience like that. Among other things, it forced me to confront the limitations of pop music and its draw. 1b. As wild as Ascension s ometimes feels, it predicates without having arrived at a music that depends foremost on collective improvisation where listening and meaningful response have overtaken chops and strutting (not that chops and strutting can’t be part of meaningful communication). What opens up, then, is the possibility for music-making where the reception of one’s own and others’ sound while playing is governed by a feeling out of the pulse of the whole, accepting contingency and accident as integral to the flow of making. Musical “intention” in this context becomes an emergent property of the experience of intersubjectivity. 1c. Most (90%?) deliberately made music appears to our ears in strict time, where the musicians aim to become part of a single organism beating in time, and their music tries to compel listeners to imaginatively join that rhythmic organism. There is solace and belonging offered in that vision of unity and unfreedom. I’ve had enough of that music. How else might we imagine and experience collective practices of meaning-making/moving/sounding as individual and collective flourishing/belonging/being-with-others? Ascension. Questionnaire 1. When did you first hear Ascension, or come to know about it? What was your response? How did this event affect your understanding of Coltrane and what he’s up to, of jazz music, and/or music and what it’s up to? 1a. How do you think about music and music‑making after Ascension? 1b. Has Ascension (or its ilk) informed your practice – of playing, of organizing, of selecting musicians, of conceptualizing the field of music? 1c. Has Ascension informed your understanding of society, or, dare I say it, the normative order(s) that govern(s) our understanding of power and human relations? 2. What question would you want to ask of yourself, of others, about John Coltrane @100? Email This BlogThis! Share to X Share to Facebook

items._cn_summary: 为纪念John Coltrane诞辰一百周年，鼓手Don Berman在西雅图重演其原创作品《Ascension Northwest》，灵感源自Coltrane 1966年的《Ascension》。作品以11位乐手编制展开，由反复循环的固定乐句串联起热烈即兴段落，间含低音提琴重奏等子组合互动。本文汇集了参演乐手围绕Coltrane《Ascension》影响的反思：法国号手Tom Varner回忆从最初被密集音响冲击、到逐渐接受并拥抱多声部同时爆发的力量之美，由此获得以极少量书面乐谱、纯粹依赖即兴者共同构筑庞大声响结构的创作自由。该演出体现了自由爵士对个体即兴与集体张力之间平衡的探索，承袭了Coltrane晚期极端自由方向的精神遗产。

items.body: The broadly ambitious Generate Music is the Prism Quartet's latest project, featuring saxophonists Timothy McAllister (soprano), Zachary Shemon (alto), Matthew Levy (tenor), and Taimur Sullivan (baritone). Formed in 1984, their mission is �To place the saxophone in unexpected contexts, expand the repertoire through new commissions, and challenge audiences.� On this eleven-track, 86-minute set, they do just that. Tyshawn Sorey | Ursula Rucker | Diane Monroe This collection includes the quartet augmented by David Gilmore (Electric guitar), David Krakauer (Klezmer clarinet), Tyshawn Sorey (Drums and percussion), Reuben Rogers (Bass), Ursula Rucker (Vocals and poetry), Susan Watts (Trumpet and vocals), and Diane Monroe (Violin). Through modern jazz arrangements, improvisations,� and spoken word, they seek to �explore the historical, cultural, and creative ties between Black and Jewish Americans.� Generate Music by PRISM Quartet, D. Gilmore, D. Krakauer, D. Monroe, R. Rogers, U. Rucker, T. Sorey, S. Watts � The opening track references �A Griot and a Cantor,� the storyteller in West African culture and the worship leader in the Jewish faith. The sonic architecture arrives with �The Unknown Common Ancestor,� which jumps between a World Saxophone Quartet-inspired sound and klezmer music with clarinet and trumpet.� � Generate Music by PRISM Quartet, D. Gilmore, D. Krakauer, D. Monroe, R. Rogers, U. Rucker, T. Sorey, S. Watts The striking and authoritative voice of Ursula Rucker narrates �Requiem for AJ.� After a dramatic overture, it sets up the narrative tension that develops across the record. Rucker tells the story of the 1964 murders of civil rights activists James Chaney, Andrew Goodman, and Michael Schwerner near Philadelphia, Mississippi. On the 60th anniversary of this American tragedy, Rucker explains that they went �to register black voters (sigh)� and then she asks us to: Look up the rest of the story if you care Do you... Care? Or do you just... Do you?� With tense dramatic irony, Rucker nonchalantly states, �Poets have queries,� and the recitation ends with emphatic repetition of �Do you?�� This ten-minute powerhouse also features the band at its best with Tyshawn Sorey�s swirling drumming and David Gilmore (not to be confused with his Pink Floyd namesake) offering one of his several fiery guitar solos. It makes a fitting single, representative of the in-your-face right-left punches of improvised jazz and honest stylized performance poetry. Generate Music by PRISM Quartet, D. Gilmore, D. Krakauer, D. Monroe, R. Rogers, U. Rucker, T. Sorey, S. Watts Highlighted throughout with bursts of klezmer, often seamlessly blended with funky jazz, the Jewish tradition is especially highlighted on �Lift Every Voice and Sing.� Originally debuted in 1900, this hymn by brothers John Rosamond Johnson and James Weldon Johnson has been called a �Negro national anthem.� Here it is translated into Yiddish by Joshua Woletzshky and sung by Susan Watts, featuring violin by Diane Monroe. �Shall I continue to lie about my sadness to keep you from yours?� asks Rucker on �Let�s All Gather & Go All Together, Shall We,� offering an optimistic way forward in a world of hate. She narrates the story of a young black man in Philadelphia, Pennsylvania, who is murdered by a Jewish pharmacist, exposing grief but also a way to get beyond it. Here and throughout, the music comments, prods, replies, and exuberantly jams out. Powerful, virtuosic, and close to the bone, Generate Music keeps its promise and takes another giant step in the evolution of the Prism Quartet. "Let us gather and all go together" by Ursula Rucker Live at World Cafe, Philadelphia on June 8, 2024 Find the artist online. items._cn_summary: 普林斯姆四重奏的最新专辑《Generate Music》以四把萨克斯为核心，联合电吉他、克莱兹默单簧管、鼓、贝斯、小号、小提琴及人声，探索非裔与犹太裔美国人在历史、文化与创造力上的纽带。开篇曲将西非格里奥说书传统与犹太教领唱意象并置，音响在爵士与克莱兹默之间跳跃。十首作品贯穿现代爵士、即兴与朗诵体诗歌，其中《Requiem for AJ》以冷静而戏剧化的叙述重提1964年密西西比州民权运动三烈士事件，质问听众的历史记忆。Tyshawn Sorey的旋转鼓击与David Gilmore的炽热吉他独奏为诗歌提供锋利配器，犹太传统在克莱兹默段落中与放克爵士无缝交融。

items.body:
Though this recording documents the work of thirteen of Belgium's most innovative ensembles, the real star is the Park Abbey located just outside Leuven and founded in 1129. Built and maintained for the purpose of quiet meditation, the abbey hosted the musicians who used the quiet surroundings to prepare and record their unique musical imaginings. The result is a mostly instrumental collection that mines the riches of Belgian folk and world music traditions, including Romani scales,
La Pump
rhythms, and accordion-based
bal-musette
flavors.
For example, Slovenian-native R�n�lius Bikar�s searing violin opens the set with �R�fuge.� He and his self-named ensemble channel pan-European Roma history.
Meanwhile, �Poor Boy� is a Django Reinhardt-inspired swing tune by Charlotte Pelgen & Bipolar Bows. Pelgen sings in English, and with her ukulele strumming sounding very much like a tenor banjo, the tune is enlivened by Lotte Remmen�s St�phane Grappelli-like fiddle lines.
The distinctive sound of the oud announces yet another musical tradition. Blending Mediterranean with Arabic sounds, the Lebanese-Belgian singer Amber Haddad and her trio, oudist Adil Benhsain and double bassist Martijn Vanbuel, spin a beguiling musical web. According to the liner notes (translated from the Dutch), �Tawazden� is about �seeking balance and finding peace within a complex environment.� Further, �the various spaces of the abbey and their murals are the direct source of inspiration.�
The accordion is especially prominent. So too is the Western classical tradition. Sounding almost Baroque, �Sacristia Invisibilis,� is another standout for me. Here, mandolinist Andries Boone is joined by Anouk Sanczuk on octave violin (sometimes called the baritone violin, tuned an octave lower than standard) and on harpsichord Sandra Van der Gucht. They create an indescribable sound you have to hear.
Throughout, the Abbey�s stone presence looms. Aur�lie Charneux�s solo clarinet piece �L'Ape Millenaria� is about a thousand-year-old bee that haunts the abbey. �Thila,� by Enara Navaira, evokes ancient Celts with a jazzy double bass and drum kit behind throat singing and Citera (a kind of Hungarian zither).
Airboxes is a duo who mix chromatic and diatonic accordions. Their offering �Abdij 1� sounds improvised. Again from the liner notes, �they share their impressions of the timelessness of monastic life.�
Despite the wide range of styles,
The Sound of the Abbey
has a coherence, perhaps informed by the artists� shared inspiration. The record is often surprising and always soothing. Three years in the making, the ensembles were lovingly recorded and mixed by Bert Huysentruyt and mastered by Pieter De Wagter from Equus Mastering. They have rendered a warm sound using the natural reverb of ancient stone provided by the project�s silent partner.

items.body: "There is no such thing as a stranger�s children." - old Ukrainian saying I�ve long been affected, indeed somewhat obsessed, by what�s happening in Ukraine, partly because of one of my favorite bands, DakhaBrakha. I went to Kyiv to see them at the time of the Maidan protests, just after the shooting by snipers of over a hundred protesters. I intentionally didn�t read this album�s booklet notes before listening, so that I could react to it without sympathetic pre-judgement, just as music. It�s strong musically and vocally by any standards, Ukrainian or otherwise. When I did then turn to the notes that translate and explain the songs, I had that rare experience, for me, of becoming moist-eyed. The songs are a mix of traditional and original. They are focused on the abduction by Russia of about 20,000 Ukrainian children who have been taken from their parents in Russian-occupied eastern Ukraine and sent to Russia, in an attempt to turn them into haters of their native land and people. It�s a heinous war crime. Marichka is a Ukrainian-Canadian singer who moves between Canada and her homeland. For this album she�s gathered two groups of musicians, one in each country. Both ensembles contribute vocals and instrumentation, mostly bowed strings, plus some bandura and piano. The group in Ukraine includes Lisa from the destroyed and invaded city of Mariupol, playing a solo on double ocarina; at 16 she was one of the stolen children but managed to return to Ukraine. Daughters of Donbas � co-led by Marichka and singer/bandurist Alina Kuzma, who shares the lead vocal role � is an all-female ensemble in Canada that tours performing these songs. �Foreign Land� is a reworking of a traditional song about the young girls who were sent away to work in foreign households - Marichka�s grandmother was one of these - that can also be taken to refer to the plight of today�s stolen children. The translation goes: A mother packed up her daughter To leave for a strange land To a strange land with strange people Oh, who will pity you, my daughter? Those who will beat me will pity me I'll never again live with you, my mother When, my daughter, should I expect you to come home? When the grass in the garden grows, my mother The grass grew and grew and began to dry The mother was waiting for her daughter to return, and began to cry Did you hear, my mother, how I came to you? How I flew as a bird above your window? How I cooed like a dove? If, my daughter, I could hear you I would open all the doors and windows To let you fly in Songs of Stolen Children by Daughters of Donbas, Alina Kuzma, Zo� Santo As befits the song, Marichka�s vocal here is gentle. But in the second track, �Rusalka,� with Alina Kuzma taking the lead vocals, things turn harsh and fierce. A rusalka is a mythical creature, a nature spirit of fields, forest and rivers, that features in traditional ritual songs. The melody of this one is by Zo� Santo and Kuzma, with lyrics drawing on tradition and the composition of Santo and 19thC Ukrainian poet and folklorist Taras Shevchenko. An ominous double-bass drone, chunking strings, a slithering vocal that moves into sections of white-voice fast recitative and expands into a soaring wild cry. The lyrics are very dark, perhaps evoking the hell of the front line: Home a hell of old growth stumps Marsh a mud of memories Don�t get bogged down in these parts Your kind won�t last a day in here While witches still fly, while roosters have yet to crow, Come here, something arises, �neath the oak something walks. A rusalka sat on a white birch, rusalky asked girls for shirts. Long fingers and nails so sharp Tongue forked round serrated teeth Moss grows down beneath her parts Weeds braided from ear to ear While witches still fly, while roosters have yet to crow, Come here, something arises, �neath the oak something walks. �Girls, my friends, give me your shirts. Though I�m thin, give me a thin one.� Here live us the backless ones Many voices of dead sons You are right to quake in fear Send your sinful children here �Who Am I� is a plea of separation and disorientation, the pain and confusion of an abducted child, contrasting �the human in me� and �the creature in me,� like an internalized riddle-song, with the refrain, in English: Who am I for you? Who am I for me? Do you know me? Really know me? �Enchantress,� passionately sung by Kuzma to her own bandura accompaniment, a girl�s lament of the loss of her brave love taken from her by the enchantress, who is an allegory of war, is based on a traditional song and uses that style of melody and lyrics, �Riddle,� sung by Marichka, reworks a traditional riddle song to be the riddles told by the grandfather of a child, 12-year-old Kira from Mariupol, who experienced the death of her father and her abduction to Russia. Her grandfather tracked her down, and brought her back, traumatized, and asked her riddles - as the notes say �to jog her memory, and remind her who she was, where her home was, and of her family�s love for her.� Songs of Stolen Children by Daughters of Donbas, Marichka �4.5.0� is a military expression for �all�s well� or �all is quiet.� The song is a message, as from a mother, to a stolen child. Marichka�s voice is cherishing: Remember this: I am with you, I am here Don't give up, I'm with you. Don't give up, I'm with you Your hope is my weapon Don't be sad, I'm with you 4.5.0. will be again �breaking into a tearing howl: And when the world's axis breaks When the sky folds like a parchment Out of nowhere her words will come� �and back to fragile reassurance �It's all right, I'm here, I'm here� "Lullaby," based on a traditional lullaby, sung by Alina Kuzma to accompaniment by her bandura and Zo� Santo's viola, starts in gentle lullaby style, but moves to a lament; it's for the stolen children and those who, as the notes put it, 'have been stolen for ever.' Songs of Stolen Children by Daughters of Donbas, Marichka �Remember, I Believe in You� is a powerful piece of harmonizing vocals and slithering strings. Here�s the story it�s based on: Yevhen lived in Mariupol with his three young children. During the siege they lived in a basement bomb shelter for months. One day, Russian soldiers entered their bomb shelter. Yevhen was taken to a filtration camp and separated from his children who were all taken to a hospital and then to Russian summer �camp�. In the filtration camp Yevhen was brutally tortured and forced to sleep standing on one leg. He tried to fall asleep, whispering prayers for his children: �Everything will be fine, I believe in you.� After his release he walked 30 kilometers to the place where his children had been taken but it was too late. They had already been sent to Moscow. Yevhen learned of this after receiving a text from one of his children who had found an unattended device. He traveled thousands of kilometers, crossed the borders of three countries, endured checks, interrogations and danger to reach Moscow and take his children home. All those days he tirelessly repeated to himself, �I believe in myself, I believe in my kids. Everything will be good.� �Another Heaven,� sung by Marichka with the ensemble in Ukraine, is inspired by another heart-rending story: Ilya was 9 years old when his mother was killed by a rocket strike right in front of him. He was taken to a hospital in occupied Donetsk, where 15 pieces of shrapnel were removed from his body without anesthesia. After he appeared in a report on Russian television, Ilya�s grandmother learned his location. She managed to bring her grandson to Kyiv, where he lives now, experiencing missile attacks every night. At age 11, he says that it is up to everyone to fight enemies, to protect other cities, and to build another heaven, where your home will not be destroyed. In 2014, during the Kyiv Maidan protests, Marichka wrote and performed �Red Boots Tango,� using a melody she�d put to a poem by Taras Shevchenko. For this album she sings it again in Ukraine, with the ensemble there adding swirling, classic tango-style strings. Songs of Stolen Children by Daughters of Donbas, BanduraGirl The final track on the album is a solo, recorded in Kyiv, by Anastasiya Voytyuk, accompanying herself on the older, simpler form of bandura that was used by kobzars to accompany epic poetry, and also on the nowadays more well-known big, heavy form developed from it in Soviet times that was made mainly in the piano factory at Chernihiv. Her song, �Soon I Will Be Back,� is based on a poem by novelist, journalist and war crime researcher Victoria Amelia, who was killed in 2023, in the city of Kramatorsk in Donbas, by a Russian rocket. Find the artist online. Further reading: Otava Yo - Do You Love (Review) Sofia Rei - Umbral (Review)

items.body:
According to its founder, Eugene Rodriguez, who also sings and plays on the record, Los Cenzontles is a �musical group and non-profit organization, which I founded over thirty years ago.�  As he continues in the album�s liner notes, the group �has a long history of producing projects exploring Mexico�s deep roots and our connections with various traditions that, so far, have included Irish, Louisiana Creole, Cuban, American cowboy, classical, pop, rock, and blues�, the latest of which is
Adios Ke Aloha: Waves of the Same Sea
. Los Cenzontles translates to the mockingbird, or, from its Aztec root word, the bird of four hundred voices. This is a fitting name for the range of musical diversity represented here.
With songs sung in Spanish, Hawaiian, and English, the concept traces back to the legacy of Mexican cowboys who travelled from California to the Hawaiian Islands to wrangle the long-horned cattle introduced there in the nineteenth century. They also brought the guitar. The 16 tracks feature old Hawaiian songs with new Spanish lyrics, old Mexican songs with new Hawaiian lyrics, new compositions, and traditional Americana. Yet it is an entirely cohesive musical package held together by dense arrangements of ukuleles, guitars, Mexican harp, and accordion.
Sonny Lim & David Hidalgo
Besides their distinctive voices, the headline artists Taj Mahal and David Hidalgo provide the gravitas and musicianship that their long and distinguished careers have earned. According to the liner notes, they were the catalysts behind the project and facilitated the choice of songs, arrangements, and played a range of instruments. On vocals they are joined by Hawaiian natives Gary Haleamau, Sheldeen Haleamau, Sonny Lim, and long-time Cenzontles member Fabiola Trujillo.
Deportee
To give a taste of the sessions, included before the traditional �Fishin� Blues� is Taj Mahal teaching the musicians how to play it. Sung by David Hildalgo,  the lovely �A Matter of Time� comes from the 1984 album
Will the Wolf Survive
by his most famous project, Los Lobos. Another standout for me, �Navegar� features a slack string guitar solo reminiscent of Duane Eddie and one of many tasty lap steel turns by Sonny Lim. Their interpretation of Woody Guthrie's �Deportee� moves into social commentary, highlighting the cruel realities of being a migrant worker in America.
Vaquero Paniolo
Recorded over five days, mostly live in one room at the Los Cenzontles headquarters in San Pablo, California, including the talents of some of their academy�s students, the recording has real spontaneity to it. Arrangements are stretched by improvisations, sometimes by several different instruments on a single tune. The project also represents a great spirit of cooperation and diversity of language, culture, age, and gender. It includes the inputs of musical legends, seasoned pros, and amateurs. The wonderfully rich and often stereotyped musical cultures of both Mexico and Hawaii are represented here with the authenticity of lived experience.
Adios Ke Aloha: Waves of the Same Sea
is a worthy addition to Los Cenzontles� important work. Quoting Rodriguez again, �Culture is a fabric within which we are all woven.�

items._cn_summary: 这是一张以墨西哥牛仔文化与夏威夷音乐传统交汇为核心概念的世界音乐跨界专辑。Los Cenzontles是一个拥有三十余年历史的音乐团体和非营利机构，致力于探索墨西哥音乐根源与多元传统的连接。专辑共16首曲目，涵盖西班牙语、夏威夷语和英语三种语言，将老夏威夷歌曲填入新西班牙语歌词，老墨西哥歌曲改编为夏威夷语版本，并融入新创作与传统美国民谣。制作邀请了Taj Mahal、David Hidalgo等资深音乐人参与演唱与编曲，并由夏威夷本地歌手和墨西哥合奏团成员协作完成。录音在加州圣巴勃罗的Los Cenzontles总部以同期方式完成，大量使用尤克里里、吉他、墨西哥竖琴与手风琴，编曲层次丰富且现场感强烈。专辑还融入社会评论，如伍迪·格斯里原作《Deportee》被重新诠释为对移民劳工处境的关注。整体呈现了跨语言、跨文化、跨代际的协作精神，是一张兼具传统根基与跨文化视野的作品。
